11.title: The Two Witnesses and the Seventh Trumpet
11.overview:
Chapter 11 is the most compressed chapter in Revelation, covering the entire church age from two angles: the measuring of the temple (the church’s preservation), the ministry of the two witnesses (the church’s prophetic witness), their death and resurrection (the church’s apparent defeat and vindication), and the seventh trumpet (the declaration of the kingdom consummated). It is also one of the most contested chapters in the book.

The measuring of the temple in vv. 1–2 has generated enormous debate. Dispensationalists understand it as a prophecy of a literal rebuilt temple in Jerusalem during the tribulation, the outer court given over to Gentile domination for 42 months. The amillennial reading understands the temple as the church (following Paul’s regular use of temple-language for the believing community — 1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21; 2 Corinthians 6:16) and the measuring as God’s preservation of his people. The outer court “given over to the nations” represents the church’s visible vulnerability to worldly power — it will be trampled — while the inner sanctuary (the true community of the redeemed) is preserved.

The two witnesses of vv. 3–13 are the most important image in the chapter. Their identity has been debated endlessly: Moses and Elijah (because of the specific powers: turning water to blood = Moses, shutting the sky = Elijah), Elijah and Enoch (the two who did not die), or — the majority Reformed reading — the whole witnessing church across the church age. The number two is the number of legal testimony (Deuteronomy 17:6; 19:15; Matthew 18:16); the two witnesses represent the complete testimony of the church to the gospel of Jesus Christ. Their supernatural powers (fire from their mouths, power over rain and waters) are the powers of the prophetic word: proclamation that both judges and saves.

The seventh trumpet of vv. 15–19 does not release a new woe but sounds the final declaration of the kingdom: “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever.” This is the answer to the Lord’s Prayer (“Your kingdom come”) and the goal toward which all of history moves. The kingdom is announced as already accomplished — the aorist tense of the verb (“has become”) indicates a completed action. What will still unfold in chapters 12–22 is the working out of what has already been declared from the throne.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: John is given a measuring rod and told to measure the temple, the altar and the worshippers — but expressly not the outer court, which is given over to the nations to trample for forty-two months. Measuring in the prophets is a legal owner marking out what is his (Ezek. 40–42; Zech. 2:1–5). Something is claimed and something is deliberately left out, and both are God’s decision.

Verses 3–4: two witnesses are granted authority to prophesy 1,260 days in sackcloth — the coarse black goat hair of mourning, not the uniform of a triumphant movement. They are the two olive trees and the two lampstands of Zechariah 4, where two olive trees feed oil straight into a lampstand and the governing word is not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit (Zech. 4:6).

Verses 5–6 give their powers, and they are two men’s résumés side by side: fire from the mouth (cf. Jer. 5:14), shutting the sky so that no rain falls — Elijah, for three and a half years (1 Kings 17:1; Luke 4:25) — and turning water to blood and striking with plagues, which is Moses in Egypt (Ex. 7:17–20).

Verses 7–8: when they have finished their testimony, the beast from the bottomless pit makes war on them, conquers them and kills them, and their bodies lie in the street of the great city that symbolically is called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified. John supplies the interpretive key himself: pneumatikōs, symbolically. Verses 9–10: for three and a half days the world gazes at the bodies, refuses them burial, and throws the only party in the book — making merry and exchanging presents, because these two prophets had been a torment.

Verses 11–12: a breath of life from God enters them and they stand on their feet (Ezek. 37:10), and a loud voice says Come up here! — the words spoken to John at 4:1 — and they go up in a cloud and their enemies watched them. Verse 13: an earthquake takes a tenth of the city and seven thousand people, and the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven. Verse 14 closes the section: the second woe has passed.
verseByVerse.theology:
Who Are the Two Witnesses?

Four answers are seriously held: Moses and Elijah, whose powers these exactly are and who stood with Christ on the mountain; Enoch and Elijah, the two men who did not die; two literal prophets still to come; and the church in its witnessing office. Three things from the text favour the last — v. 4 calls them the two lampstands, and 1:20 has already defined a lampstand as a church; two is the legal minimum for valid testimony (Deut. 19:15), and their whole activity is testimony; and seven lampstands have become two, which suits a church reduced but still lawfully able to testify. This commentary takes that reading without dismissing the others, and on any of them the substance is the same: God has witnesses, they are given authority, they speak for a bounded time, they are killed, and they are raised.

The Temple Measured — Where Godly Readers Differ

The literal reading takes vv. 1–2 as a temple building in Jerusalem, in the dispensational understanding one still to be rebuilt (Walvoord, MacArthur), and has the merit of the plain sense; its chief difficulty is that John wrote around AD 95, a quarter of a century after the temple was destroyed and never rebuilt. The symbolic reading takes the temple as the people of God, which is the standing New Testament usage (1 Cor. 3:16; Eph. 2:21; 1 Pet. 2:5), and makes the measuring the sealing of chapter 7 in another figure.

Forty-Two Months

The book’s most repeated number, in three interchangeable forms: forty-two months (11:2; 13:5), 1,260 days (11:3; 12:6), and a time, and times, and half a time (12:14). All three are three and a half years, and all come from Daniel 7:25. Three and a half is half of seven — in a book where seven means completeness, the number of a period that is real, severe, and definitively cut off before it can run its course.

The Beast “Conquers” Them

The verb in v. 7 is nikaō, the word that ends every one of the seven letters as a promise to the faithful and is used of Christ at 5:5. Here it is used of the beast, against the saints, successfully — as it will be again at 13:7. Revelation will not pretend the church always wins its battles. It says plainly that the church loses, visibly, in public. And the whole book exists to redefine what that means, because the definitive instance of conquering by being killed is the Lamb standing in the middle of the throne with his throat cut.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Leaving a body unburied was the last insult the ancient world had; burial was owed even to an enemy, and refusing it said a person did not count as human. And the celebration in v. 10 is the only party in Revelation. Every other rejoicing in the book is in heaven; this one is in a street, because two preachers are dead, and somebody has declared a public holiday.

Now: Verse 7 carries a promise a Christian can put weight on, and it is not the promise most people want. When they have finished their testimony — the beast cannot touch them until the testimony is complete. It does not say the witness will be protected. It says the witness will be finished. Nobody in God’s service is cut off mid-sentence by accident, and the man who dies at forty with half his work apparently undone has, on the testimony of this verse, completed it.

And v. 10 gives the church a warning and a comfort in the same sentence. The warning: if the world is entirely comfortable with what your congregation says, it is not saying what these two were saying — a witness that torments nobody is probably not a witness. Ahab put it to Elijah in three words: Is it you, you troubler of Israel? (1 Kings 18:17). The comfort: when Christians are treated as a problem to be removed rather than an opinion to be debated, that is not evidence something has gone wrong. It is the treatment the two witnesses received, in the same city where their Lord received it.

Then vv. 11–13 show what actually reaches the world, and it is not what most churches would have guessed. Plagues did not do it; 9:20 says the survivors of a third of mankind dying did not repent. What did it was two witnesses in mourning dress who would not stop talking, were killed for it, and were raised in front of the people who killed them — and nine tenths of a city gave glory to the God of heaven. The vindication came after the humiliation, and in front of the same audience.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I was given a measuring rod like a staff, and I was told, "Rise and measure the temple of God and the altar and those who worship there, but do not measure the court outside the temple; leave that out, for it is given over to the nations, and they will trample the holy city for forty-two months.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I was given a measuring rod like a staff, and I was told, “Rise and measure the temple of God and the altar and those who worship there, but do not measure the court outside the temple; leave that out, for it is given over to the nations, and they will trample the holy city for forty-two months.”

Measuring in the prophets is not surveying. It is the act of a legal owner marking out what is his and what he intends to protect. Ezekiel was shown a man with a measuring reed who measured a temple for nine chapters (Ezek. 40–42). Zechariah saw a man with a measuring line going to measure Jerusalem, and was told the city would be so full that it needed no walls, for I will be to her a wall of fire all around (Zech. 2:1–5). To be measured is to be claimed.

What is being measured here is disputed, and the readings should be given straight.

The literal reading takes this as a temple building in Jerusalem — in the dispensational understanding, one still to be rebuilt, with the events here belonging to a future tribulation. This is the reading of Walvoord and MacArthur, and it has the merit of taking the plain sense of the words. The chief difficulty is dating: on the usual view John wrote around AD 95, a quarter of a century after the temple was destroyed and never rebuilt, so a literal reading requires a temple that does not yet exist.

The symbolic reading takes the temple as the people of God, which is the standing New Testament usage — do you not know that you are God’s temple? (1 Cor. 3:16; cf. Eph. 2:21; 1 Pet. 2:5). On this reading the measuring is the sealing of chapter 7 in another figure, and the two halves of the vision say one thing: the church is protected in what it truly is, and exposed in what can be reached by force.

That second point is the pastoral heart of the passage on any reading, and it is worth stating carefully. Something is measured, and something is deliberately left unmeasured, and both are God’s decision. He does not say the outer court is beyond his reach. He says leave that out, and then it is given over — the divine passive again. The trampling is licensed.

So the church is not promised that nothing can be trampled. It is promised that what the trampling can reach is not the temple. Buildings burn, reputations are ruined, denominations collapse, believers are imprisoned and killed. None of that touches the sanctuary, the altar, or the worshippers, and God has drawn the line himself with a measuring rod.

Forty-two months. This is the first appearance of the book’s most repeated number, and it arrives in three interchangeable forms: forty-two months (11:2; 13:5), 1,260 days (11:3; 12:6), and a time, and times, and half a time (12:14). All three are three and a half years, and they come from Daniel, where the little horn wears out the saints for a time, times, and half a time (Dan. 7:25; cf. 12:7).

Three and a half is half of seven. In a book where seven is the number of completeness, half of seven is the number of a period that is real, severe, and definitively not complete — broken off before it can run its course. Whether it is read as a literal future span or as the whole age of the church’s witness under pressure, its message is the same and it is the reason John keeps repeating it: this is a bounded time. Somebody has already written down when it stops.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will grant authority to my two witnesses, and they will prophesy for 1,260 days, clothed in sackcloth." These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I will grant authority to my two witnesses, and they will prophesy for 1,260 days, clothed in sackcloth.

Who are they? This is one of the more open questions in the book, and four answers are seriously held.

Some take them as Moses and Elijah, because the powers described in the next two verses are precisely theirs — shutting the sky, turning water to blood, striking with plagues — and because those two stood with Christ on the mount of transfiguration (Matt. 17:3). Some take them as Enoch and Elijah, the two men in Scripture who did not die (Gen. 5:24; 2 Kings 2:11), and who might therefore still have a death owing. Some take them as two literal prophets still to come, raised up during a future tribulation.

And many take them as the church in its witnessing office. Three things point that way, and they are drawn from the text rather than imported. First, verse 4 calls them the two lampstands, and this book has already defined a lampstand: the seven lampstands are the seven churches (1:20). Second, the number two is the legal minimum for valid testimony — only on the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses shall a charge be established (Deut. 19:15) — and their whole activity here is testimony. Third, seven lampstands have become two, which suits a church reduced but still lawfully able to testify.

This commentary takes the last reading, without dismissing the others. And on any of them the substance of the passage is unchanged: God has witnesses, they are given authority, they speak for a bounded time, they are killed, and they are raised.

Note what they are wearing. Clothed in sackcloth — coarse black goat hair, the dress of mourning and repentance, worn by Jacob for a dead son and by Nineveh at Jonah’s preaching. This is not the uniform of a triumphant movement. It is the clothing of people who are grieved by what they see and are calling for repentance, and it tells you the tone of the church’s testimony in this age. Not swagger. Mourning.

These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth. The image is lifted whole from Zechariah 4, where the prophet sees a golden lampstand with a bowl on top and two olive trees beside it feeding oil directly into the lamps. He asks twice what they mean and is told: These are the two anointed ones who stand by the Lord of the whole earth (Zech. 4:14) — in Zechariah, Joshua the high priest and Zerubbabel the governor, the two men rebuilding a ruined temple in a ruined city.

And the word that vision turns on is the sentence spoken to Zerubbabel in the middle of it: Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of hosts (Zech. 4:6). That is the point of the olive trees. A lampstand cannot make light and cannot make oil; it holds up what is poured into it. The church testifying in sackcloth for 1,260 days is not running on its own reserves, and never was.

Which is the answer to a discouragement common to every serious Christian: the sense that the church is too small, too tired and too compromised to say anything the world will hear. The two witnesses are two, in mourning dress, in a city that will kill them. They are also connected by a pipe to an inexhaustible supply, and the authority they have was granted.

verseByVerse.quote: And if anyone would harm them, fire pours from their mouth and consumes their foes. If anyone would harm them, this is how he is doomed to be killed. They have the power to shut the sky, that no rain may fall during the days of their prophesying, and they have power over the waters to turn them into blood and to strike the earth with every kind of plague, as often as they desire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And if anyone would harm them, fire pours from their mouth and consumes their foes. If anyone would harm them, this is how he is doomed to be killed.

Fire from the mouth, not from the hand. In this book that is a settled image: the sword proceeds from the mouth of Christ (1:16; 19:15), and Jeremiah was told Behold, I am making my words in your mouth a fire, and this people wood, and the fire shall consume them (Jer. 5:14). The weapon is the word. What these witnesses do is speak.

The sentence is stated twice, which is unusual and deliberate. It reads like a standing legal rule rather than a description of an event: harm them, and this is what follows. And the second half is passive — he is doomed to be killed — so the witnesses are not the executioners. They speak; the judgment falls from somewhere else.

Then the powers themselves, and they are two men’s résumés laid side by side. They have the power to shut the sky, that no rain may fall during the days of their prophesying — that is Elijah exactly, who told Ahab there would be neither dew nor rain except by his word, and there was not, for three and a half years (1 Kings 17:1; Luke 4:25; James 5:17). And they have power over the waters to turn them into blood and to strike the earth with every kind of plague — that is Moses in Egypt (Ex. 7:17–20).

And notice the duration Luke and James both attach to Elijah’s drought: three and a half years. The number of this chapter, arriving in the source material.

Moses and Elijah stand behind the two witnesses whether or not they are the two witnesses, and the pairing is not random. They are the law and the prophets, the two halves of the Old Testament, and they are the two figures who appeared with Christ on the mountain and spoke with him about his departure (Luke 9:30–31). What the church testifies to is the whole word of God, and it is doing what Moses and Elijah did — standing in front of a Pharaoh and an Ahab and saying the true thing.

The phrase as often as they desire is startling and should not be softened into something more modest. God does not give his witnesses a rationed supply of authority for approved occasions. But hold it beside verse 7, which is coming, and the shape of the whole passage appears: these are people with power to shut the sky, and they are about to be killed in the street, and both of those things are true at once.

That combination is the actual experience of the church in every century, and it is why this passage matters to an ordinary congregation. The word of God in the mouth of believers has real, world-altering force — and the people who carry it are frequently overpowered, humiliated and killed. Anyone who has only been told the first half will be shattered by the second. Anyone who has only seen the second will not believe the first. John gives both, two verses apart.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they have finished their testimony, the beast that rises from the bottomless pit will make war on them and conquer them and kill them, and their dead bodies will lie in the street of the great city that symbolically is called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they have finished their testimony, the beast that rises from the bottomless pit will make war on them and conquer them and kill them.

Four words carry the whole verse, and the first one changes everything: when they have finished. The beast does not interrupt them. He cannot touch them until the testimony is complete. Whatever else is true about the church’s vulnerability, no witness in this book is silenced before he has said what he was sent to say.

That is a promise a Christian can put weight on, and it is not the promise most people want. It does not say the witness will be protected. It says the witness will be finished. Nobody in God’s service is cut off mid-sentence by accident, and the man who dies at forty with half his work apparently undone has, on the testimony of this verse, completed it.

Then the beast, and this is his first appearance in the book — introduced casually, with a definite article, two chapters before he is described. He rises from the bottomless pit, the shaft opened in 9:1–2, which places him: he is not a rival power from somewhere else. He comes up out of a hole that has to be unlocked with a key that somebody was given.

And now the word that ought to stop a reader: he will conquer them. It is nikaō, the verb that ends every one of the seven letters as a promise to the faithful, the verb used of Christ himself in 5:5. Here it is used of the beast, against the saints, successfully — and it will be used that way again at 13:7, where the beast is allowed to make war on the saints and to conquer them.

Revelation will not pretend the church always wins its battles. It says plainly that the church loses, visibly, in public, at the hands of a power that is permitted to defeat it. And the whole book exists to redefine what that means — because the definitive instance of somebody conquering by being killed is the Lamb standing in the middle of the throne with his throat cut (5:6). The beast conquers by killing witnesses. The Lamb conquered by being killed. Same verb, opposite direction.

And their dead bodies will lie in the street of the great city that symbolically is called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified.

Note that John supplies the interpretive key himself: symbolically — the Greek is pneumatikōs, spiritually, in the manner of the Spirit. He is telling the reader outright that these names are not addresses.

Where their Lord was crucified points to Jerusalem. Sodom is the byword for depravity, and Isaiah had already called Jerusalem’s rulers you rulers of Sodom (Isa. 1:10). Egypt is the house of slavery that would not let God’s people go. And the great city is a phrase this book will use again and again — of Babylon (17:18; 18:10). Piling four identities onto one city is the point: wherever the people of God are opposed, that place becomes Sodom and Egypt and Babylon and the city that killed the Lord. It is one city under many names, and it has a branch in every generation.

Their bodies lie in the street. Not in a prison, not in a tomb — in the open, where the traffic goes. Whatever public humiliation looks like in a given century, that is what is being described, and John does not spare the reader a single detail of it.

verseByVerse.quote: For three and a half days some from the peoples and tribes and languages and nations will gaze at their dead bodies and refuse to let them be placed in a tomb, and those who dwell on the earth will rejoice over them and make merry and exchange presents, because these two prophets had been a torment to those who dwell on the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For three and a half days some from the peoples and tribes and languages and nations will gaze at their dead bodies and refuse to let them be placed in a tomb.

Three and a half days this time, against three and a half years everywhere else in the chapter. The proportion is the message: the humiliation is real and it is brief. It has the same shape as the ministry and none of the length.

To leave a body unburied was, in the ancient world, the last insult available. Burial was owed even to an enemy; refusing it was a way of saying that a person did not count as human. And the fourfold phrase — peoples, tribes, languages, nations — is the one used since 5:9 of the ransomed multitude, now used of the spectators. The same world that the Lamb bought is standing in the street looking at the bodies.

The verb is gaze, not glance. They come and stand and look, for three and a half days, at two corpses. There is a particular kind of public appetite being described here, and any generation that has watched a humiliation circulate for days will recognise it exactly.

And those who dwell on the earth will rejoice over them and make merry and exchange presents, because these two prophets had been a torment to those who dwell on the earth.

This is the only party in the book of Revelation. Every other celebration in these chapters is in heaven; this one is on the earth, and it is held because two preachers are dead. Exchange presents is the detail that makes it unbearable — it is the language of a festival, a public holiday. Somebody declares a day off. People send each other gifts.

And John gives the reason without flinching: because these two prophets had been a torment to those who dwell on the earth. The word is the one used of the locusts tormenting people in 9:5. The witnesses had no army and no legal standing; what they had was a message, and the message was intolerable. Ahab said it to Elijah in three words: Is it you, you troubler of Israel? (1 Kings 18:17).

There is a warning in that for the church and a comfort in it, and they are the same sentence. The warning: if the world is entirely comfortable with what your congregation says, it is not saying what these two were saying. A witness that torments nobody is probably not a witness. The comfort: when Christians find themselves treated as a problem to be removed rather than an opinion to be debated, that is not evidence that something has gone wrong. It is the treatment the two witnesses received, and the treatment their Lord received in the same city.

And note the phrase, three times in two verses: those who dwell on the earth. John’s technical term, established at 8:13, for people whose whole account is settled here. They are throwing a party in a street, and it lasts three and a half days, and the next verse begins with the word but.

verseByVerse.quote: But after the three and a half days a breath of life from God entered them, and they stood up on their feet, and great fear fell on those who saw them. Then they heard a loud voice from heaven saying to them, "Come up here!" And they went up to heaven in a cloud, and their enemies watched them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But after the three and a half days a breath of life from God entered them, and they stood up on their feet, and great fear fell on those who saw them.

The wording is Ezekiel’s, and any reader who knows the valley of dry bones will hear it immediately. The prophet was set down in a valley full of bones, very many and very dry, and asked whether they could live; and he was told to prophesy to them, and breath came into them and they lived and stood on their feet, an exceedingly great army (Ezek. 37:1–10). The Greek word for breath here is pneuma, which is also the word for Spirit, and the ambiguity is in the Hebrew of Ezekiel too.

What was declared finished by a public that had refused it burial stands up in the street. And the detail John records is the reaction of the crowd: great fear fell on those who saw them. The party stops mid-sentence. Three and a half days of gazing at corpses, and then the corpses stand up.

Then they heard a loud voice from heaven saying to them, “Come up here!” And they went up to heaven in a cloud, and their enemies watched them.

Every phrase in that sentence has been used before in this book or in the Gospels, and the effect is cumulative. Come up here is exactly what the trumpet voice said to John at 4:1. In a cloud is how Christ ascended, a cloud taking him out of the disciples’ sight (Acts 1:9), and how he will return (1:7). The witnesses are given their Lord’s death, in his city, and then their Lord’s resurrection and his ascension, in that order.

And the last clause is not decoration: and their enemies watched them. When Jesus rose, the world did not see it; the guards saw an empty tomb and were paid to say something else, and the risen Christ appeared only to his own. Here the vindication is public, and the people who arranged the deaths are standing in the street with their gifts still in their hands.

Which is where this passage does its real work for an ordinary believer. The pattern it describes is not that faithful witness avoids humiliation. It is that the vindication comes after, and in front of the same audience. Every Christian who has been written off, misrepresented, quietly removed, or made ridiculous for saying something true is being shown the end of that story, and the end of it is not a private consolation. It is a summons heard out loud and a departure the accusers have to watch.

Note also what the witnesses do not do. They do not argue, retaliate, or explain. They stand up, and they are called, and they go. Vindication in Scripture is almost never something a person achieves; it is something done to him by somebody else, usually later than he would have chosen. Peter told churches in these same provinces exactly that: humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God so that at the proper time he may exalt you (1 Pet. 5:6).

verseByVerse.quote: And at that hour there was a great earthquake, and a tenth of the city fell. Seven thousand people were killed in the earthquake, and the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven. The second woe has passed; behold, the third woe is soon to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And at that hour there was a great earthquake, and a tenth of the city fell. Seven thousand people were killed in the earthquake, and the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven.

The proportions are the first thing to notice, because they run the opposite way from everything in the book so far. In chapter 6 a fourth of the earth was struck. In chapters 8 and 9 it was a third, repeatedly. Here it is a tenth, and seven thousand die — and the remaining nine tenths do something no group in Revelation has done yet.

The rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven.

Set that against 9:20, four columns earlier: the rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent. Same phrase, opposite outcome. The trumpets of chapter 9 struck a third of mankind and produced nothing. Two witnesses prophesied in sackcloth, were killed, and were raised — and nine tenths of a city gave glory to God.

Whether that is genuine conversion is debated, and honesty requires saying so. Some read it as terror rather than repentance, noting that in 16:9 people who refuse to repent are said to have cursed God rather than glorified him, so the contrast is deliberate but perhaps only formal. Others — and the wording is on their side — take it at face value: gave glory to the God of heaven is what Revelation says of real worship (14:7; 16:9 negatively; 19:7), and this is the one place in the book where a mass of ordinary people turns to God.

If that reading is right, and it probably is, the chapter has made an argument about how the world is actually reached, and it is not the argument most churches would have made. Plagues did not do it. Cosmic catastrophe did not do it. A third of mankind dying did not do it. What did it was two witnesses in mourning dress, refusing to stop talking, being killed for it, and being raised.

The number seven thousand may carry an echo. When Elijah — who stands behind these witnesses — complained that he alone was left, God told him he had kept seven thousand in Israel, all the knees that have not bowed to Baal (1 Kings 19:18). There, seven thousand were the remnant preserved. Here, seven thousand fall and a great multitude is preserved. The arithmetic of grace has been turned the other way up.

The second woe has passed; behold, the third woe is soon to come. The bookkeeping verse again, matching 9:12. The eagle’s three woes of 8:13 are the fifth, sixth and seventh trumpets, and two of the three are now behind. The third is announced as soon, and the very next verse sounds the seventh trumpet — which turns out to contain no woe at all that John records, only the announcement of a kingdom.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 15: the seventh trumpet sounds and brings no plague at all, only an announcement — The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever. Singular kingdom, not plural: one worldly system under many governments, and it has changed hands. And the verb is aorist, a completed act: not will become but has become.

Verses 16–17: the twenty-four elders come off their own thrones onto their faces, giving thanks to Lord God Almighty, who is and who was — and the threefold title of 1:4, 1:8 and 4:8 has lost its third term. The one who is to come has come, and the future tense drops out of the name of God. You have taken your great power and begun to reign: not been given, but taken. He was always sovereign; what changes is that the reign becomes visible and unopposed.

Verse 18 quotes Psalm 2:1 in the past tense — the nations raged, and it is over — and lists what the moment contains: wrath; the dead judged; the servants rewarded, the prophets and saints, and those who fear your name, both small and great; and destroying the destroyers of the earth, an exact reciprocity using the same root twice.

Verse 19 opens the temple in heaven, and the ark of his covenant was seen within his temple — the object that stood behind the veil, seen by one man once a year, and lost when Babylon destroyed the temple in 586 BC. Then the storm signs, now five of them: lightning, rumblings, thunder, earthquake and heavy hail.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Outcome Is Announced at the Halfway Point

The most important structural fact about Revelation is in v. 15. The kingdom is declared to have changed hands with eleven chapters still to run — before the dragon appears, before either beast rises, before Babylon falls and before the white horse rides out. This book is not a thriller in which the ending is in doubt. It is the account of a war whose result was announced at the halfway point, and before that at an empty tomb. The congregations who first heard it were not being asked to hope for a victory; they were being asked to live inside one that had not yet been made visible.

A Word Left Out

The divine title has been threefold since the first chapter: who is and who was and who is to come. At the seventh trumpet it is twofold. Nothing in the chapter says more than that omission, and it is said by leaving a word out.

Reward Is Not a Contradiction of Grace

Verse 18 says God intends to reward his servants, and the New Testament is entirely unembarrassed about it (Matt. 6:4; 1 Cor. 3:14; Heb. 11:6). Grace is not the abolition of reward; it is the reason a reward is possible at all. And the generosity of the clause is its point: three overlapping groups, ending with a phrase that refuses to let anybody be ranked out of it — both small and great. The witnesses who shut the sky and the widow who kept praying and never told anybody are in the same sentence.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: For six hundred years the holiest object in Israel’s worship had simply been gone. The ark vanished when Babylon burned the temple, and Jeremiah said a day would come when nobody would say the ark of the covenant of the LORD any more, nor miss it (Jer. 3:16). Verse 19 opens the doors of the temple in heaven and there it is, in plain view. The covenant was not lost when the building fell; God has kept his side of it; and the place where blood was applied for a nation’s sin is still in the room.

Now: The chapter opens by measuring and closes by opening a temple, and between the two it is honest about what can be trampled. The church is not promised that nothing will be lost. Buildings burn, reputations are ruined, denominations collapse, believers are imprisoned and killed. What is promised is that the trampling cannot reach the sanctuary, the altar, or the worshippers — and that God drew the line himself, with a measuring rod, before anything was given over.

And the discouragement this passage answers is a real one: the sense that the church is too small, too tired and too compromised for the world to hear anything it says. The two witnesses are two, in mourning dress, in a city that will kill them. They are also connected by a pipe to an inexhaustible supply, and the authority they have was granted. A lampstand cannot make light and cannot make oil. It holds up what is poured into it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the seventh angel blew his trumpet, and there were loud voices in heaven, saying, "The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever." And the twenty-four elders who sit on their thrones before God fell on their faces and worshiped God, saying, "We give thanks to you, Lord God Almighty, who is and who was, for you have taken your great power and begun to reign.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the seventh angel blew his trumpet, and there were loud voices in heaven, saying, “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever.”

Six trumpets brought hail, blood, wormwood, darkness, locusts and cavalry. The seventh brings an announcement, and it is the sentence the whole book has been climbing towards. Any reader who knows Handel has heard these words sung, and the singing can carry a person past what they actually say.

The kingdom of the world. Singular, not plural. Not the kingdoms, as the older translations had it — there is one worldly kingdom under many governments, one system, and it has changed hands.

Has become. The verb is aorist, a completed act, and it is the tense that makes the sentence extraordinary. Heaven does not announce that the kingdom of the world will become God’s, or is in the process of becoming his. It announces a transfer that has already happened. This is the language of a herald reading out a result, not a forecast.

And it is announced at the seventh trumpet, with eleven chapters of the book still to run. The dragon has not appeared yet. Neither beast has risen. Babylon has not fallen and the white horse has not ridden out. The outcome is declared before the conflict is described, which is the single most important structural fact about Revelation. The book is not a thriller in which the ending is in doubt. It is the account of a war whose result was announced at the halfway point, and before that at an empty tomb.

Consider what that meant to the congregations who first heard it. They were being read a document that told them the empire would get worse, that a beast would be given authority over every tribe and people, that they would be conquered and killed. And in the middle of it, loud voices in heaven saying that the kingdom of the world has already changed owner. They were not being asked to hope for a victory. They were being asked to live inside one that had not yet been made visible.

And the twenty-four elders who sit on their thrones before God fell on their faces and worshiped God, saying, “We give thanks to you, Lord God Almighty, who is and who was, for you have taken your great power and begun to reign.”

And here is the small detail that repays every minute spent on it. The divine title in this book has been threefold from the first chapter: who is and who was and who is to come (1:4, 8; 4:8). Here it is twofold. Who is and who was — and the third term is gone.

It is not an oversight. The one who is to come has come. The title had a future tense in it for as long as there was a future to wait for, and at the seventh trumpet the waiting ends and the tense drops out of the name of God. Nothing in the chapter says more, and it is said by leaving a word out.

You have taken your great power and begun to reign. Not been given — taken. He was always sovereign; what changes here is that the reign becomes visible and unopposed. The one who is and who was has stopped being patient, and the elders’ response is not analysis. Twenty-four figures who have thrones of their own get off them and put their faces on the floor.

verseByVerse.quote: The nations raged, but your wrath came, and the time for the dead to be judged, and for rewarding your servants, the prophets and saints, and those who fear your name, both small and great, and for destroying the destroyers of the earth." Then God's temple in heaven was opened, and the ark of his covenant was seen within his temple. There were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, an earthquake, and heavy hail.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The nations raged, but your wrath came, and the time for the dead to be judged, and for rewarding your servants, the prophets and saints, and those who fear your name, both small and great, and for destroying the destroyers of the earth.

The nations raged is a quotation. Psalm 2 opens with it: Why do the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain? — and goes on to describe kings setting themselves against the LORD and against his Anointed, and God laughing, and installing his King on Zion. Revelation has been quoting that psalm since 2:27. Here it reports it in the past tense. The raging is over. It was answered.

Then four things the moment contains, and each needs its own moment.

Your wrath came. Stated in a single clause and not dwelt on, in a book that has spent six chapters on judgment. The point of the list is elsewhere.

And the time for the dead to be judged. Everyone, without exception, including everyone who died believing the matter was closed. Nothing has been filed away.

And for rewarding your servants, the prophets and saints, and those who fear your name, both small and great. This is the longest clause in the verse, and its generosity is the point. Three overlapping groups — prophets, saints, and simply those who fear your name — and then a phrase that refuses to let anybody be ranked out of it: both small and great. There is no tier system at this reward. The two witnesses who shut the sky and the widow who kept praying and never told anybody are in the same sentence.

And rewarding is the word. Not merely vindicating or receiving. God intends to give things to people for what they did, and the New Testament is entirely unembarrassed about that (Matt. 6:4; 1 Cor. 3:14; Heb. 11:6). Grace is not the abolition of reward; it is the reason a reward is possible at all.

And for destroying the destroyers of the earth. The judgment is stated as an exact reciprocity, and the same Greek root is used twice, which the English preserves. The people who ruined the world are themselves ruined. Nothing arbitrary is happening: the sentence is the crime, said back.

Then God’s temple in heaven was opened, and the ark of his covenant was seen within his temple.

Stop at that, because for a Jewish reader it would have been the most astonishing sentence in the chapter. The ark of the covenant stood in the Most Holy Place, behind the veil, and exactly one man saw it once a year. It disappeared when Babylon destroyed the temple in 586 BC and was never seen again; Jeremiah had said the day would come when people would no longer say the ark of the covenant of the LORD, nor miss it (Jer. 3:16). For six hundred years the holiest object in Israel’s worship had been simply gone.

Here it is. In the temple in heaven, in plain view, with the doors open. The ark was the box that held the covenant — the tablets of the law — under a lid where blood was sprinkled once a year. To see it standing there is to be told that the covenant was never lost when the building fell, that God has kept his side of it, and that the place where blood was applied for a nation’s sin is still in the room. The chapter that began by measuring a temple and leaving part of it to be trampled ends by opening the real one.

And then the storm: flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, an earthquake, and heavy hail. John’s standing signal that God has acted, used at 4:5 with three elements, at 8:5 with four, and here with five. It grows each time. The nations raged; his wrath came; the covenant stands open in the light; and the last sound in the chapter is thunder over an ark that nobody had seen for six hundred years.

There were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, an earthquake, and heavy hail.

12.title: The Woman, the Dragon, and the War in Heaven
12.overview:
Chapter 12 is the theological heart of Revelation. Everything that has come before — the seals, the trumpets, the witnesses — and everything that follows — the beasts, the bowls, Babylon’s fall — is explained here. We are shown the cosmic backstory: the war between the dragon and the woman, the birth of the child who will rule all nations, the war in heaven that cast Satan down, and the dragon’s fury against the woman’s offspring. This is the explanation for why the church is persecuted: the dragon, having failed to destroy the child, turns his fury on those who “hold to the testimony of Jesus.”

The great sign in heaven — the woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars — draws on Genesis 37:9 (Joseph’s dream where the sun, moon, and eleven stars bowed down to him, representing his family) and on the Old Testament imagery of Israel as the bride/mother of God’s people (Isaiah 54; Jeremiah 6:2). The woman is not Mary (though the imagery encompasses the incarnation). She is the messianic community — Israel who gave birth to the Messiah, and the church who is the continuation and expansion of that community. She is clothed with cosmic glory; she is in labor.

The great red dragon with seven heads and ten horns and seven diadems is Satan himself, identified explicitly in v. 9: “that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world.” His seven heads and ten horns anticipate the beast of chapter 13, which mirrors the dragon’s appearance — the beast is the dragon’s instrument, Rome as the embodiment of satanic opposition to Christ. The dragon’s tail sweeping down a third of the stars has been interpreted as the fall of the angels who followed Satan in the primordial rebellion.

The cosmic war of vv. 7–12 is one of the most dramatic scenes in Revelation: Michael and his angels fight the dragon and his angels; the dragon is thrown down. The war in heaven is won. The announcement that follows is the theological explanation: they conquered “by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death.” The cross — not Michael’s sword — is the decisive weapon. The dragon is thrown down because the Lamb was slain.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Woman and the Dragon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: a great sign — John says so before he describes anything — a woman clothed with the sun, the moon under her feet, a crown of twelve stars, pregnant and screaming in labour. The sun, moon and twelve stars come from Joseph’s dream, where Jacob himself supplies the key (Gen. 37:9–10): this is the covenant people, from whom the Messiah comes.

Verses 3–4: another sign, a great red dragon with seven heads, ten horns and seven diadems — royal crowns, not the victor’s wreath the woman wears, and the crowns that belong by right to the rider of 19:12. His tail sweeps down a third of the stars, and he stands in front of the woman waiting to devour the child.

Verse 5: she bears a male child who is to rule all the nations with a rod of iron (Ps. 2:9) — and the child is caught up to God and to his throne. Between the birth and the throne there is nothing: no Galilee, no cross, no empty tomb. Thirty-three years pass in a comma, because from the dragon’s side there is nothing to report but total failure.

Verse 6: the woman flees into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, to be nourished for 1,260 days. The child is safe on the throne; the mother is in the desert — which is the position of the church between the ascension and the end.
verseByVerse.theology:
Who Is the Woman?

Some have taken her as Mary, and a real woman really did bear the child of v. 5. But this woman survives the ascension, flees for 1,260 days, and has other offspring who keep the commandments of God (v. 17). That is not a biography. She is the covenant people — Israel, out of whom Christ came, and then the church, which is the same people continued.

The Plot of the Old Testament in One Sentence

Verse 4 — the dragon waiting to devour the child at birth — is Genesis 3:15 running through the whole Old Testament. Cain kills Abel. Pharaoh orders the Hebrew boys into the Nile. Athaliah destroys the royal family of Judah and misses one baby hidden in a bedroom (2 Kings 11:1–3). Haman gets a decree against every Jew in the empire. And Herod sends soldiers to Bethlehem. Matthew reports the massacre as history; John shows what was underneath it.

Two Pictures of One Church

The woman is clothed with the sun and screaming in agony at the same time, and both are accurate. Seen from heaven the church is crowned with stars; seen from the street she is a woman in labour, alone, making a great deal of noise. A believer shown only the first will not recognise his own congregation; one shown only the second will not believe there is anything else to see. And birth pain in Scripture is never merely suffering — it is suffering with an outcome (Isa. 26:17; Matt. 24:8; Rom. 8:22). Nobody labours for nothing.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The dragon of the Old Testament is the chaos-monster of the deep — Leviathan, Rahab, the twisting serpent God alone can master (Job 41; Ps. 74:13–14; Isa. 27:1) — and Ezekiel called Pharaoh the great dragon that lies in the midst of his streams (Ezek. 29:3). A congregation hearing this read would have understood at once that the thing standing behind their magistrate was very old and had been beaten before.

Now: This chapter offers what almost nothing else in Scripture gives so directly: the second layer. The events are real — a real decree, a real sword, real children — and there is something behind them that is also real, hostile, personal, and has been at this a very long time. Paul said it without the picture: we do not wrestle against flesh and blood (Eph. 6:12).

And v. 6 names a place many Christians have lived in without knowing what it was. The wilderness is where Israel went after the exodus and was fed for forty years by bread that arrived each morning; where Elijah was fed by ravens and by an angel (1 Kings 17:6; 19:5–8). It is a hard address and it is not abandonment. The accommodation was booked — a place prepared, the same verb as John 14:2 — and the feeding is done by a hand the verse does not name.

verseByVerse.quote: And a great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars. She was pregnant and was crying out in birth pains and the agony of giving birth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The book turns here. Chapters 1 to 11 have shown what happens on earth and in heaven as the scroll is opened; chapter 12 pulls the curtain back further and shows why — the war behind the war. From here to chapter 20 the reader is looking at the dragon, his two beasts, and their city, and this chapter introduces all of it.

And a great sign appeared in heaven. The word is sēmeion, a sign — something that stands for something else. John says so before he describes anything, which is his standing courtesy to the reader: this is a sign, read it as one.

A woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars.

Who is she? The imagery answers it, and the answer is not the one many readers expect. Joseph dreamed of the sun, the moon and eleven stars bowing down to him, and his father understood it immediately: the sun was Jacob, the moon was his mother, and the stars were his brothers (Gen. 37:9–10). Add Joseph and you have twelve. The sun, the moon and twelve stars is Israel — the covenant people from whom the Messiah comes.

Some readers have taken the woman to be Mary, and she is certainly in the picture: a real woman really gave birth to the child of verse 5. But the woman of this chapter survives the child’s ascension, flees into the wilderness, is pursued for 1,260 days and has other offspring who keep the commandments of God (v. 17). That is not a biography. She is the covenant people of God — Israel, out of whom Christ came, and then the church, which is the same people continued.

She is clothed in glory and she is in agony, and both at once. She was pregnant and was crying out in birth pains and the agony of giving birth. John does not soften it. The word for her cry is the word used of a person screaming.

That combination is the whole doctrine of the people of God in one picture, and it is why this chapter matters to an ordinary congregation. Seen from heaven, the church is clothed with the sun and crowned with stars. Seen from the street, she is a woman in labour making a great deal of noise, alone, with something enormous waiting for her. Both are accurate. A believer who has only been shown the first picture will not recognise his own church; one who has only seen the second will not believe there is anything else to see.

And birth pain in Scripture is never merely suffering. It is suffering with an outcome. Isaiah used it of Israel in exile (Isa. 26:17–18; 66:7–9); Jesus used it of the troubles preceding the end — all these are but the beginning of the birth pains (Matt. 24:8); Paul used it of the whole creation groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now (Rom. 8:22). Nobody labours for nothing. The pain is real, it is severe, and it is going somewhere.

verseByVerse.quote: And another sign appeared in heaven: behold, a great red dragon, with seven heads and ten horns, and on his heads seven diadems. His tail swept down a third of the stars of heaven and cast them to the earth. And the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, so that when she bore her child he might devour it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And another sign appeared in heaven: behold, a great red dragon, with seven heads and ten horns, and on his heads seven diadems.

A sign again, and John says so again. This is not what Satan looks like; it is what Satan is, rendered in a picture. The dragon in the Old Testament is the chaos-monster of the deep — Leviathan, Rahab, the twisting serpent that God alone can master (Job 41; Ps. 74:13–14; Isa. 27:1) — and Ezekiel called Pharaoh the great dragon that lies in the midst of his streams (Ezek. 29:3).

Every detail is a counterfeit of something already seen in this book. Seven heads: seven is God’s number of completeness, and the dragon wears it. Ten horns: horns are power, and ten is fullness of a lesser kind. Seven diadems — and this is the sharpest detail. A diadēma is a royal crown, not the stephanos given to victors; the woman wears a stephanos of stars, and the dragon wears seven royal crowns. He is claiming sovereignty he does not hold, and at 19:12 the rider on the white horse will appear wearing many diadems, which settles the question of who the crowns actually belong to.

His tail swept down a third of the stars of heaven and cast them to the earth. Read most naturally in the light of verses 7 to 9, this is the angels who fell with him. A third — the same fraction that has run through the trumpets. Even in the account of his greatest success the dragon gets a limited portion, and two thirds stayed.

And the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, so that when she bore her child he might devour it.

That single sentence is the plot of the Old Testament. Immediately after the fall God promised enmity between the serpent and the woman, and between his offspring and hers, and said he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel (Gen. 3:15). Everything after that is the serpent trying to get to the child first. Cain kills Abel. Pharaoh orders every Hebrew boy thrown into the Nile. Athaliah destroys the whole royal family of Judah and misses one baby hidden in a bedroom (2 Kings 11:1–3). Haman obtains a decree to destroy every Jew in the empire. And when the child is finally born, Herod sends soldiers to Bethlehem to kill every boy under two.

Every one of those is the dragon standing in front of the woman with his mouth open. Matthew reports Herod’s massacre as history; John shows what was underneath it.

And that is what this chapter offers a reader that no other part of Scripture offers quite so directly: the second layer. The events are real — a real decree, a real sword, real children — and there is something behind them that is also real, and hostile, and personal, and has been at this for a very long time. Paul said the same thing without the picture: we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness (Eph. 6:12).

Note where he is standing, though, and how little he does. He stands before the woman, waiting. He has seven crowns he did not earn and a mouth open for a child not yet born. In the next verse the child is taken to the throne of God, and the dragon does not lay a finger on him.

verseByVerse.quote: She gave birth to a male child, one who is to rule all the nations with a rod of iron, but her child was caught up to God and to his throne, and the woman fled into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, in which she is to be nourished for 1,260 days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She gave birth to a male child, one who is to rule all the nations with a rod of iron, but her child was caught up to God and to his throne.

The identification is settled by the quotation. You shall break them with a rod of iron and dash them in pieces like a potter’s vessel is Psalm 2:9, the coronation psalm of the Messiah, which this book has already applied to Christ and to those who conquer (2:27) and will apply again at 19:15. The child is Jesus.

And then the most extraordinary compression in Scripture. Between she gave birth and caught up to God and to his throne there is nothing. No childhood, no Galilee, no Sermon on the Mount, no miracles, no cross, no empty tomb. Thirty-three years and the entire Gospel narrative pass in a comma.

Why? Because of what this chapter is showing. It is not telling the story of Jesus; it is telling the story of the dragon’s attempt on him, and the point being made is that the attempt failed completely. From the dragon’s side there is nothing to report between the birth and the throne except a total defeat. He stood there with his mouth open and the child went straight past him to the seat of God.

The verb is caught up — hērpasthē, snatched, seized with force. It is the word Paul uses of the man caught up to the third heaven (2 Cor. 12:2) and of the church caught up to meet the Lord (1 Thess. 4:17). Its sense is a rescue performed at speed. Whatever the dragon intended, the child was removed out of reach.

And be clear about what that does and does not mean, because the compression can mislead. It does not mean the cross was avoided. The cross is in this book everywhere — the Lamb standing as though slain is the central image of the whole vision, and the very next paragraph will say the saints conquered the dragon by the blood of the Lamb. It means the cross was not a victory for the dragon. He devoured nothing. The child he was waiting for went to the throne, and the route ran through a grave that could not hold him.

And the woman fled into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, in which she is to be nourished for 1,260 days.

The child is safe on the throne; the mother is in the desert. That is the position of the church between the ascension and the end, and every word of the sentence is carefully chosen.

The wilderness is where Israel went after the exodus — the place of danger, of no resources, and of daily provision, where a nation was fed for forty years by bread that arrived each morning. It is where Elijah was fed by ravens and by an angel (1 Kings 17:6; 19:5–8). It is a hard address and it is not abandonment.

A place prepared by God — the same verb used of the place Christ has gone to prepare (John 14:2). The desert was not an accident of flight; the accommodation was booked. And she is to be nourished, passive, by somebody not named, for the 1,260 days that this book keeps repeating. The church in this age is a woman in a desert being fed by an unnamed hand for a period that has already been measured.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Satan Thrown Down to Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 7–8: war in heaven, Michael and his angels against the dragon and his; the dragon fights back, is defeated, and there was no longer any place for them in heaven. Michael appears in Scripture only in Daniel, Jude and here — the great prince who has charge of your people (Dan. 12:1), and the archangel who would not pronounce a blasphemous judgment against the devil but said The Lord rebuke you (Jude 9).

Verse 9 gives him four names in one sentence, and each is a job description: the great dragon, raw destructive power; that ancient serpent, the same one, from the garden; the devil, diabolos, slanderer; and Satan, Hebrew for adversary or accuser. Two of the four mean the same thing. He is also the deceiver of the whole world, and the verb thrown down is repeated three times in the verse.

Verse 10 explains it, and the explanation is a court case: the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down, who accuses them day and night before our God. Verse 11 defines the book’s central verb in three clauses — they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death. Verse 12 gives the two reactions: heaven rejoices, earth and sea are warned, for the devil has come down to you in great wrath, because he knows that his time is short.
verseByVerse.theology:
When Was the War?

Three positions are held: before Genesis 1, as the original rebellion; at the end, still future; or at the cross and resurrection. The passage itself points to the third, since v. 10 dates the expulsion by saying now the salvation and the kingdom of our God have come, and v. 11 grounds the victory in the blood of the Lamb. Jesus said both I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven (Luke 10:18) and now will the ruler of this world be cast out (John 12:31).

What Was Satan Doing in Heaven?

The Old Testament answers it, and the answer is the key to the chapter. In Job he presents himself among the sons of God and accuses a righteous man to his face (Job 1:9). In Zechariah he stands at the right hand of the high priest to accuse him — and the priest is in filthy garments and the accusation is true (Zech. 3:1–4). His place in heaven was never a throne. It was a prosecutor’s bench.

The Definition of “Conquer”

Every one of the seven letters ends with a promise to the one who conquers, and v. 11 says what that consists of, in order. By the blood of the Lamb — the ground of everything: the accuser was not defeated by an argument or by the saints’ record, but because the charges were paid, and a prosecutor whose every allegation has already been settled has nothing left to do in the room. By the word of their testimony — what they said. They loved not their lives even unto death — the cost. Christian courage does not begin with bravery. It begins with a verdict already delivered in blood.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Verse 11 was written to congregations in which people had already died, and it does not tell them that faithfulness would have kept them alive. It tells them that the deaths were how the accuser was beaten — that a person who is no longer holding on to his own life has nothing left that can be threatened.

Now: Take v. 10 as literally as it is written, because it names something a great many Christians experience and cannot account for. There has been, in the presence of God, a voice reciting a list — and not inventing charges. That is the terrible part: the file in Zechariah 3 was accurate, and the high priest really was standing there in filthy clothes. The accusations are, on the whole, true, and they were being read out day and night for as long as the accuser had standing in the room.

He has been thrown out — not because the charges failed and not because God stopped listening, but because they were paid. Which means that the voice a believer still hears reciting his record is no longer a prosecutor with standing. It is somebody shouting through a door he has been put outside of.

And v. 12 reframes the pressure itself. The devil’s great wrath is not the confidence of an advancing enemy; the verse says plainly why he is furious — because he knows that his time is short. A cornered animal is dangerous precisely because it is cornered.

verseByVerse.quote: Now war arose in heaven, Michael and his angels fighting against the dragon. And the dragon and his angels fought back, but he was defeated, and there was no longer any place for them in heaven. And the great dragon was thrown down, that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world—he was thrown down to the earth, and his angels were thrown down with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now war arose in heaven, Michael and his angels fighting against the dragon. And the dragon and his angels fought back, but he was defeated, and there was no longer any place for them in heaven.

Michael is named in Scripture only in Daniel, Jude and here. In Daniel he is the great prince who has charge of your people (Dan. 12:1; cf. 10:13, 21), and Jude calls him an archangel who, disputing with the devil about the body of Moses, would not pronounce a blasphemous judgment but said The Lord rebuke you (Jude 9). He is a creature, and a careful one.

When did this war happen? The question is real and the answer decides how the chapter is read. Three positions are held. Some place it before Genesis 1, as the original rebellion. Some place it at the end, still future. And many place it at the cross and resurrection — which is where the passage itself points, since verse 10 dates the expulsion by saying now the salvation and the kingdom of our God and the authority of his Christ have come, and verse 11 says the saints conquered him by the blood of the Lamb.

Jesus said something that fits exactly. When the seventy came back reporting that even the demons were subject to them, he answered I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven (Luke 10:18). And on the last night he said now is the judgment of this world; now will the ruler of this world be cast out (John 12:31). Whatever else happened at the cross, something was thrown out of a position it had held.

Which raises a question a thoughtful reader will already have: what was Satan doing in heaven at all? The Old Testament answers it plainly, and the answer is the key to the whole chapter. In Job he presents himself among the sons of God and accuses a righteous man to his face: Does Job fear God for no reason? (Job 1:9). In Zechariah he stands at the right hand of the high priest to accuse him, and the priest is wearing filthy garments and the accusation is true (Zech. 3:1–4). Satan’s place in heaven was never a throne. It was a prosecutor’s bench.

And the great dragon was thrown down, that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world — he was thrown down to the earth, and his angels were thrown down with him.

Four names in one verse, and each one is a job description. The great dragon — the chaos-monster, raw destructive power. That ancient serpent — and the adjective is doing work: this is the same one, from the garden, and John expects the reader to make the connection to Genesis 3 without help. The devil, diabolos, which means slanderer. Satan, which is Hebrew for adversary or accuser. Two of the four names mean the same thing, and the next verse will make that the point.

The deceiver of the whole world. That is his method, and it has not changed since the first conversation in the garden, which was not a threat but a question: Did God actually say? He is not primarily described in this book as a torturer or a tempter. He is a liar with a legal practice.

And the verb is repeated three times in one verse: thrown down… thrown down… thrown down with him. He did not withdraw, resign, or lose interest. He was removed, and he was removed by force, and the sentence will not stop saying so.

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard a loud voice in heaven, saying, "Now the salvation and the power and the kingdom of our God and the authority of his Christ have come, for the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down, who accuses them day and night before our God. And they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death. Therefore, rejoice, O heavens and you who dwell in them! But woe to you, O earth and sea, for the devil has come down to you in great wrath, because he knows that his time is short!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I heard a loud voice in heaven, saying, “Now the salvation and the power and the kingdom of our God and the authority of his Christ have come, for the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down, who accuses them day and night before our God.”

Heaven explains what has just happened, and the explanation is entirely about a court case. The dragon is not called the tempter here, or the destroyer, or the ruler of this world. He is the accuser of our brothers, and the participle is present and continuous: who accuses them day and night before our God.

Take that as literally as it is written, because it explains something a great many Christians experience and cannot name. There has been, in the presence of God, a voice reciting a list. Not inventing charges — that is the terrible part; the prosecutor’s file in Zechariah 3 was accurate, and the high priest really was standing there in filthy clothes. The accusations against you are, on the whole, true. And they were being read out, day and night, for as long as the accuser had standing in the room.

He has been thrown out. Not because the charges failed, and not because God stopped listening. Look at the next verse for the reason.

And they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death.

This is the definition of the book’s central verb, and everything in the seven letters depends on it. Conquer has been promised to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia and Laodicea. Here is what it consists of, in three clauses.

By the blood of the Lamb. First, and it is the ground of the other two. The accuser was not defeated by an argument, and certainly not by the saints’ record. He was defeated because the charges were paid. A prosecutor whose every allegation has already been settled by somebody else has nothing to do in the room. That is why he is outside; there is no case left to bring.

And by the word of their testimony. Second, and it follows from the first. What they said. Not what they achieved — they say the true thing about Christ in front of people who do not want to hear it, and that saying is a weapon.

For they loved not their lives even unto death. Third, and it is the cost. The phrase does not mean they hated living. It means that when it came to a choice between their lives and their testimony, the testimony won. Some of them died for it. That is what put the matter beyond the accuser’s reach: a person who is not holding on to his own life has nothing left that can be threatened.

Read those three clauses in order and the shape of Christian courage appears. It does not begin with bravery. It begins with a verdict already delivered in blood, produces speech, and only then costs something. Nobody in this verse is asked to be fearless first.

Therefore, rejoice, O heavens and you who dwell in them! But woe to you, O earth and sea, for the devil has come down to you in great wrath, because he knows that his time is short!

The same event produces opposite reactions in the two places, and John holds both. Heaven celebrates; earth is warned. And the reason given for the devil’s great wrath is not that he is winning. It is that he knows that his time is short.

That single clause reframes a great deal of Christian experience. The pressure a believer feels is not the pressure of an advancing enemy; it is the fury of one who has been thrown out of the courtroom, has read the timetable, and has very little left. A cornered animal is dangerous precisely because it is cornered. And short here is the same family of words as the soon of 1:1 — short as heaven measures it, which is not always short as a suffering church measures it, and is short nonetheless.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — The Dragon Pursues the Woman
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 13: when the dragon saw that he had been thrown down, he pursued the woman. The logic matters — he goes after the mother because he cannot reach the child, who is on the throne, and cannot go back to the courtroom.

Verse 14: the woman was given the two wings of the great eagle to fly into the wilderness, to be nourished for a time, and times, and half a time. The wings are the exodus — I bore you on eagles’ wings and brought you to myself (Ex. 19:4; cf. Deut. 32:11; Isa. 40:31) — and the time is Daniel 7:25, the third form of the same number John has now used three ways in two chapters.

Verses 15–16: the serpent pours a river out of his mouth to sweep her away, and the earth came to the help of the woman and swallowed it — as the ground opened on Korah (Num. 16:31–33) and the sea closed over Pharaoh’s chariots.

Verse 17: the dragon, furious, goes off to make war on the rest of her offspring — reaching back to Genesis 3:15 — defined by exactly two marks: those who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus. And the chapter ends on a quiet, ominous line: And he stood on the sand of the sea.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Complete Exodus

By the end of the chapter every element is present: a tyrant trying to kill the children, a child rescued, a flight, a wilderness, a place prepared, food from an unnamed hand, eagles’ wings, and a water-crossing in which the enemy is defeated by the flood he intended. John is telling congregations under Roman pressure that they are living inside the book of Exodus, and that they already know how it ends.

The Flood from the Mouth

What comes out of the dragon’s mouth is what always comes out of it: he was called the deceiver of the whole world six verses earlier, and his one method is speech. In the Psalms, overwhelming waters are the standard image for slander and hostile testimony (Ps. 69:1–2, 15). A flood is a good picture of how a reputation is destroyed — not one accusation, which can be answered, but a volume of it arriving faster than anyone can respond, until the truth is simply under water. And the rescue comes from the least likely quarter: in this book the earth is usually where the trouble is.

Two Marks, and Only Two

Verse 17 defines the dragon’s targets with unusual precision, and the shortness of the list is the challenge in it. Not those who understand this book. Not those who identified the beast correctly. Not those who never suffered. Obedience — in the things God actually commanded rather than the things a person would prefer to be judged on — and confession, held on to. That is the whole description, and it is all it takes to be on his list.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The last sentence of the chapter is a manuscript question the ESV footnotes: some copies read I stood, which would make it John standing on the shore rather than the dragon, and would join the sentence to 13:1. The better reading is he. The dragon walks down to the shoreline and stands looking out at the water — and the next sentence in the book is And I saw a beast rising out of the sea. He is calling something up, and chapters 12 and 13 are one movement.

Now: The persecution of the church in this age is the displaced rage of a defeated prosecutor. That does not make it less real, and this book never pretends it does. What it settles is what the pressure means: it is not evidence that the dragon is gaining ground, but that he has lost the only ground that mattered and has nowhere else to go.

And the wilderness is described a second time as a place of nourishment rather than exposure. Any Christian who has been through a stretch of life with nothing in it — no prospects, no company, no visible progress — is being told what that place is for. It is not where God loses track of his people. It is where he feeds them without competition.

So the reader arrives at chapter 13 with everything he needs to watch it without panic. The child is on the throne. The accuser has been thrown out and has no case to bring. The woman is fed in a place prepared for her. The saints conquer by blood already shed and words already spoken. And the dragon on that beach, about to summon the worst thing in the book, is a defeated prosecutor with a short time, doing the only thing left to him.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the dragon saw that he had been thrown down to the earth, he pursued the woman who had given birth to the male child. But the woman was given the two wings of the great eagle so that she might fly from the serpent into the wilderness, to the place where she is to be nourished for a time, and times, and half a time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the dragon saw that he had been thrown down to the earth, he pursued the woman who had given birth to the male child.

Catch the logic of the verse. He goes after the woman because he has been thrown down. He cannot reach the child, who is on the throne. He cannot go back to the courtroom. So he turns on the mother, and the persecution of the church in this age is the displaced rage of a defeated prosecutor.

That does not make the persecution less real, and this book never pretends it does. What it does is settle what the persecution means. It is not evidence that the dragon is gaining ground. It is evidence that he has lost the only ground that mattered and has nowhere else to go.

But the woman was given the two wings of the great eagle so that she might fly from the serpent into the wilderness.

The image is the exodus, and John expects it to be recognised at once. God said to Israel at Sinai: You yourselves have seen what I did to the Egyptians, and how I bore you on eagles’ wings and brought you to myself (Ex. 19:4). Moses used it again in his last song, of an eagle that stirs up its nest and spreads its wings and catches its young and bears them on its pinions (Deut. 32:11).

So the chapter now has a complete exodus in it: a tyrant trying to kill the children, a child rescued, a flight, a wilderness, a place prepared, food from an unnamed hand, eagles’ wings, and in the next verse a water-crossing where the enemy is defeated by the flood he intended. This is not decoration. John is telling seven congregations under Roman pressure that they are living in the book of Exodus, and that they already know how it ends.
