verseByVerse.quote: No longer will there be anything accursed, but the throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, and his servants will worship him. They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads. And night will be no more. They will need no light of lamp or sun, for the Lord God will be their light, and they will reign forever and ever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The removal of the curse — ‘no longer will there be anything accursed’ — is the reversal of Genesis 3:14–19 and Deuteronomy 28. The curse that fell on the serpent, on the ground, on the woman, on the man — removed. Not merely covered, not merely forgiven, not merely managed — removed. The creation that was subjected to futility (Romans 8:20) is released from its bondage. The groaning of creation (Romans 8:22) is silenced. The curse is gone.

Seeing God’s face is what theology calls the beatific vision — the direct, immediate, unmediated knowledge of God that the creatures of earth were made for but have been unable to access since the fall. Moses could not see it; Isaiah was undone by a glimpse; Daniel fell as dead at a partial vision. Now the servants of God see it directly, permanently, without dying. This is the consummation of salvation: not merely being forgiven, not merely being made holy, but being brought into the direct presence of the God who is love and light and beauty, and finding there the satisfaction of every longing that was ever placed in the human heart.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The final section of Revelation is a cascade of voices, testimonies, warnings, and invitations. The angel certifies the truth of the visions (‘these words are trustworthy and true’). Jesus speaks in the first person three times: ‘I am coming soon’ (vv. 7, 12, 20). The sixth beatitude of the book falls: ‘Blessed is the one who keeps the words of the prophecy of this book.’ John falls at the angel’s feet and is corrected: ‘Worship God.’ The seal of the book is refused — unlike Daniel (Daniel 12:4), John is told not to seal the words of the prophecy, because the time is near.

The self-identification of Jesus in v. 13 — ‘I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end’ — is the full trinitarian echo of 1:8 (where the same title belongs to the Lord God Almighty). Jesus is the Alpha and Omega alongside and equal to the Father. He is the one who was before creation began and will be when creation is complete; he is the interpretive key to all that lies between. The final blessing and the final warning (vv. 14–15) restate the binary of the whole book: those who wash their robes have the right to the tree of life; those whose lives are defined by the excluded vices remain outside.

The final invitation (v. 17) is the most open, the most generous, the most inclusive statement in the entire book: ‘The Spirit and the Bride say, “Come.” And let the one who hears say, “Come.” And let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who desires take the water of life without price.’ After all the warnings, all the judgments, all the exclusions — the door is still open. The water is still free. The invitation still stands. Come.

The book closes with the third ‘I am coming soon’ from Jesus and the church’s great response: ‘Amen. Come, Lord Jesus.’ Maranatha — ‘Come, Lord’ in Aramaic — is one of the earliest Christian prayers (1 Corinthians 16:22; Didache 10:6). It is the prayer the church has been praying for two thousand years. Every generation of the church since the first has prayed it expecting the Lord’s return in their own lifetime; every generation has passed on to those who followed the same prayer, the same hope, the same expectation. We pray it still. We pray it with them. Come, Lord Jesus.
verseByVerse.theology:
The refusal to seal the book (v. 10) — ‘Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near’ — contrasts with Daniel 12:4 (‘shut up the words and seal the book, until the time of the end’). Daniel was sealed because the fulfilment was far off; Revelation is unsealed because the fulfilment is near. In the eschatological framework of the New Testament, the ‘last days’ began at Pentecost (Acts 2:17); the church has lived in the last days ever since. Every generation is the generation for whom the book was unsealed.

The title ‘Root and Descendant of David, the bright morning star’ (v. 16) combines the two lines of Jesus’ identity: he is the Root of David (the one from whom David sprang — the eternal Son who precedes the king) and the Descendant of David (the one who comes from David’s line — the human heir to the throne). He is simultaneously the source and the fulfilment of the Davidic covenant. And the morning star — promised to the overcomers in 2:28 — is now revealed as Jesus himself: the light that heralds the dawn, the sign that the long night is over.
verseByVerse.examples:
The warning of vv. 18–19 against adding to or taking from the words of the prophecy of this book is the strongest statement of canonical finality in the New Testament. It does not mean that Revelation is the only inspired book; it means that the revelation of God in Jesus Christ is complete, sealed, and inviolable. Every generation faces the temptation to add to the gospel (making it more palatable, more impressive, more culturally acceptable) or to take from it (removing the parts that are offensive or difficult). Both additions and subtractions are equally forbidden.

The final prayer of the Bible — ‘Come, Lord Jesus’ — is the prayer that orients the whole Christian life. To pray this prayer sincerely is to acknowledge that the present age is not the final one, that the best is yet to come, that the world as it is now is not the world as it will be. It is the prayer of hope, the prayer of longing, the prayer of those who have tasted enough of the kingdom to be hungry for its fullness. The church that has stopped praying ‘Come, Lord Jesus’ has stopped living as a pilgrim community. The church that prays it regularly lives with its face toward the horizon.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to me, "These words are trustworthy and true. And the Lord, the God of the spirits of the prophets, has sent his angel to show his servants what must soon take place." "And behold, I am coming soon. Blessed is the one who keeps the words of the prophecy of this book."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The double certification — the angel confirming the trustworthiness of the visions, then Jesus speaking in the first person — forms a double seal of authority on the whole book. ‘Trustworthy and true’ is a title belonging to Christ himself (3:14; 19:11); when the angel applies it to the words of the book, he is identifying the book’s authority with Christ’s own authority. The book of Revelation is not the vision of an excited mystic; it is the word of the one who is trustworthy and true.

The sixth beatitude of the book falls on ‘the one who keeps the words of the prophecy.’ Keeps — not merely reads, not merely understands, not merely debates. The book’s blessing falls on obedience. The same word appears in 1:3 (the first beatitude): the book begins and ends with the same call. The whole arc of Revelation is: hear it, keep it, endure.

verseByVerse.quote: I, John, am the one who heard and saw these things. And when I heard and saw them, I fell down to worship at the feet of the angel who showed them to me, but he said to me, "You must not do that! I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers the prophets, and with those who keep the words of this book. Worship God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John falls at the angel’s feet a second time (the same mistake occurred in 19:10). The repetition is not carelessness; it is the honest acknowledgment that even the apostle who wrote ‘God is love’ and ‘we shall see him as he is’ could, in the overwhelming presence of divine glory mediated through an angel, misplace his worship. The angel’s correction is immediate and firm: ‘Worship God.’ Two words in Greek. The simplest, most direct command in the book.

The angel identifies himself as ‘a fellow servant’ with John, the prophets, and all who keep the words of the book. Angels are not objects of worship; they are fellow worshippers, fellow servants of the same God. This is the great levelling of heaven: apostles and angels and prophets and ordinary believers — all of them servants of the same Lord, all of them pointing away from themselves toward the same God.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to me, "Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near. Let the evildoer still do evil, and the filthy still be filthy, and the righteous still do right, and the holy still be holy."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The unsealing of the book is the statement that the fulfilment is near. Daniel was told to seal his vision; John is told to unseal his. The difference is the incarnation: the things Daniel saw from a distance are now near, because the one who is Alpha and Omega has entered history, died, and risen. Every generation since Pentecost has lived in the ‘time is near’ of Revelation 22:10.

The apparently resigned instruction of v. 11 — ‘let the evildoer still do evil’ — is not permission for sin but a statement about eschatological hardening: at the very end, the choices people have made become permanent. The one who has persistently chosen evil finds that character has set. The one who has persistently chosen holiness finds that character has set. This is the final expression of the truth that runs through all of Revelation: the present choices shape the eternal character.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, I am coming soon, bringing my recompense with me, to repay each one for what he has done. I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second ‘I am coming soon’ is accompanied by the declaration of the final judgment: ‘bringing my recompense with me, to repay each one for what he has done.’ The return of Christ is simultaneously the consummation of redemption and the completion of justice. He comes to give the redeemed their inheritance and the condemned their verdict — the same coming, the same moment, the two sides of one final act.

The threefold self-identification — Alpha and Omega, first and last, beginning and end — is the most emphatic statement of Christ’s deity in the book. All three phrases describe the one who stands outside time as its source and goal. He was before the beginning and will be after the end. Nothing exists that is not encompassed by him. The same Lord who opened history will close it; the same word that spoke creation into being will speak the new creation into being.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have the right to the tree of life and that they may enter the city by the gates. Outside are the dogs and sorcerers and the sexually immoral and murderers and idolaters, and everyone who loves and practices falsehood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The seventh and final beatitude of Revelation falls on those who ‘wash their robes’ — the language of 7:14 (‘they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb’). The right to the tree of life is granted not to those who earned it but to those who received the cleansing that is freely offered. The washing is an act of grace received through faith; the result is the right — exousia, the legal authority — to enter and eat.

The outside of the city — those excluded — is described not as a place of torment in this passage but as the place of absence: outside the gates, outside the light, outside the tree of life. The exclusion is itself the judgment. Those who have defined their lives by falsehood, idolatry, and the vices of Babylon are outside the city because they chose what was outside the city; they have received what they pursued.

verseByVerse.quote: "I, Jesus, have sent my angel to testify to you about these things for the churches. I am the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus speaks in the first person, naming himself: ‘I, Jesus.’ Not ‘the Lord’ or ‘the Alpha and Omega’ — but the human name, the name of the one born in Bethlehem, the name that means ‘YHWH saves.’ The whole book — with all its cosmic visions, its heavenly throne rooms, its cosmic battles — is sent by Jesus to the churches. It is a pastoral letter from the risen Lord to his struggling congregations.

The Root and Descendant of David fulfils the double strand of messianic prophecy: he pre-exists David as the divine Son from whom the Davidic line derives its meaning (Matthew 22:41–46; John 8:58), and he descends from David as the promised heir of the covenant (Matthew 1:1; Romans 1:3). He is simultaneously the source and the fulfilment of every promise. The morning star — promised to the overcomer in 2:28 and now revealed as Jesus himself — is the sign that the night is nearly over.

verseByVerse.quote: The Spirit and the Bride say, "Come." And let the one who hears say, "Come." And let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who desires take the water of life without price.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This single verse contains the most beautiful invitation in the Bible. Three parties call: the Spirit (who throughout Revelation speaks to the churches and longs for the consummation — Romans 8:26–27), the Bride (the church, which longs for its Lord — the consummation of the relationship promised in chapters 19 and 21), and then every hearer who joins the invitation by passing it on. The ‘Come’ is directed both toward Jesus (the prayer of longing for his return) and toward the thirsty (the invitation to come and drink).

The water of life without price is the last and greatest expression of free grace in the Bible. Isaiah 55:1 (‘come, buy and eat, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price’) is fulfilled here: the water that sustains eternal life costs the recipient nothing. It cost the giver everything — the blood of the Lamb, the suffering of the cross, the groaning of all creation. But at the point of receiving, it is free. All you need is thirst. All you need is desire. Come.

verseByVerse.quote: I warn everyone who hears the words of the prophecy of this book: if anyone adds to them, God will add to him the plagues described in this book, and if anyone takes away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God will take away his share in the tree of life and in the holy city, which are described in this book.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The warning against addition and subtraction echoes Deuteronomy 4:2 and 12:32 (‘you shall not add to the word that I command you, nor take from it’), applying the canonical finality of the Mosaic law to the book of Revelation and, by extension, to the whole canon of Scripture of which it is the culmination and seal. The word of God is sufficient; it is complete; it requires neither supplementation nor revision.

The sanctions — the plagues of the book for those who add; loss of the tree of life for those who subtract — are the two forms of the binary that runs through the whole book. Those who add to the gospel (presenting a different Christ, a different grace, a different salvation) walk into the judgments of the book. Those who subtract from it (softening the exclusivity of Christ, removing the reality of judgment, eliminating the hard demands of holiness) lose the inheritance. Both the adding and the taking away are forms of the deception that the whole book has warned against.

verseByVerse.quote: He who testifies to these things says, "Surely I am coming soon." Amen. Come, Lord Jesus! The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third and final ‘I am coming soon’ from Jesus receives the church’s great Amen — ‘so be it, yes, truly’ — and then the prayer that the whole New Testament has been building toward: ‘Come, Lord Jesus.’ Maranatha in its Greek translation. The earliest Christians prayed it in Aramaic (1 Corinthians 16:22; Didache 10:6). Every generation since has prayed it in their own language. We pray it still. It is the prayer that confesses the incompleteness of the present age and the certainty of its completion; the prayer that holds together patience (we wait) and longing (we come); the prayer that is simultaneously the church’s deepest desire and its clearest confession of faith.

The grace benediction — ‘the grace of the Lord Jesus be with all’ — is the final word of the Bible. Not warning, not instruction, not prophecy — grace. The book that has shown more visions of divine justice than any other ends with grace. The last word of Scripture is the word that sums up everything God has done in Jesus Christ: undeserved, freely given, sufficient for every need, available to all who come to the water of life without price. Amen.

15.title: The Song of Moses and the Lamb
15.overview:
Chapter 15 is the shortest chapter in Revelation — eight verses — but it is one of the most carefully constructed. It serves as the vestibule to the seven bowl visions of chapter 16, doing what chapters 4–5 did before the seals and what chapters 8:1–5 did before the trumpets: grounding the coming sequence in the worship and sovereignty of God before a single bowl is poured. Before heaven acts in judgment, heaven first breaks into song.

The chapter presents two contrasting scenes held in deliberate tension. The first (vv. 1–4): the victorious on the sea of glass, harps in hand, singing the Song of Moses and the Lamb. The second (vv. 5–8): seven angels emerge from the heavenly temple dressed for a solemn task, given seven golden bowls by one of the four living creatures, while the temple fills with the glory of God so completely that no one can enter until the seven bowls are finished. Praise and solemn purpose belong together. The song is not premature celebration; it is the theological foundation without which the coming acts of God would be misread.

The Song of Moses and the Lamb is one of the richest theological moments in the book. It binds together the two great saving acts of God — the Exodus and the cross — into a single song of praise. The God who opened the Red Sea is the God who opened the tomb. The Lamb who was slain is the LORD who drowned Pharaoh’s army. The song the victorious sing is drawn almost entirely from the Psalms, Jeremiah, and Deuteronomy — the whole Hebrew Scripture gathered into the church’s final praise.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — The Song of the Victorious
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 1: another sign in heaven, great and amazing — the third and last of the book’s three signs, after the woman (12:1) and the dragon (12:3). Seven angels with seven plagues, which are the last, for with them the wrath of God is finished. The verb is from teleō, the same root as the word from the cross, It is finished (John 19:30).

Verse 2: the sea of glass of 4:6 is now mingled with fire, and standing beside it are those who had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name, holding harps — a direct contradiction of 13:7, where the beast was allowed to conquer them. The position is the far shore of the Red Sea with Egypt behind it.

Verses 3–4: they sing the song of Moses… and the song of the Lamb — one song under two names. Its words are not from Exodus 15 but are a mosaic of Scripture: Great and amazing are your deeds (Ps. 111:2), Just and true are your ways (Deut. 32:4), Who will not fear you, O King of the nations? (Jer. 10:7), All nations will come and worship you (Ps. 86:9). Four clauses, and every one is about God — not one word about the beast, the persecution, or their own endurance.
verseByVerse.theology:
Wrath Has an End; Mercy Does Not

A reader six chapters into dragons and beasts might reasonably fear that the wrath of God is a reservoir with no bottom — that once it starts it simply continues. Verse 1 says the opposite before a single bowl is lifted: there is a last plague, after which there are no more. Scripture says his steadfast love endures for ever and never once says that of his anger (Ps. 30:5; Mic. 7:18). Judgment in the Bible always has a stopping-point written into it; grace does not. And if the wrath of God against sin is a thing that can be finished, the question worth asking is where it was finished for a Christian — and the same author used the same verb of a hill outside Jerusalem.

Conquered, and Conquering

At 13:7 the beast conquers the saints; at 15:2 the saints have conquered the beast. Same verb, opposite direction, same encounter — and holding both together is the single most important thing this book asks of a suffering Christian. From the street the beast won, and there is no version of events in which the believers were not arrested and killed. From the sea of glass they won, and they are standing with instruments in their hands. 12:11 has already explained the mechanism: the winning was not survival but refusing to let go.

Worship Made of Quotations

The redeemed of heaven sing in Scripture. Not one line of their song is original to them; it is stitched together out of the psalms and the prophets they were given, which is a quiet argument for filling a mind with them now. What a person sings at the end is what he had in him.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Israel stood on the far bank of the sea with Pharaoh’s army at the bottom of it and sang. John puts this company beside the sea before he tells us what they sing, so that a congregation hearing it read would make the connection before the words arrived. Israel came out of Egypt through water; these came out of the beast’s empire through fire and death; and it is the same song, because the God who did the first did the second.

Now: Verse 2 lists what they conquered in three parts — the beast and its image and the number of its name — and not one of them is an army. It is a demand. They were not asked to defeat anything; they were asked not to bow, not to worship an image, and not to take a number that would have let them keep trading. Their whole victory consists of things they did not do.

Say that plainly to any Christian who suspects his own faithfulness is too passive to count. The company standing on the sea of glass with harps did not storm anything. They declined — repeatedly, at increasing cost — and heaven files that under conquered.

And their song is the answer to their own question. Under the altar in 6:10 they cried how long? Here the first thing they say about the way God ran history is that it was just and true. No complaint and no question — not because the question was never asked, but because it has been answered.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw another sign in heaven, great and amazing, seven angels with seven plagues, which are the last, for with them the wrath of God is finished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I saw another sign in heaven, great and amazing, seven angels with seven plagues, which are the last, for with them the wrath of God is finished.

This is the shortest chapter in Revelation, and it does one job: it gets the reader ready. Chapter 16 will pour out seven bowls in twenty-one verses, faster and heavier than anything in the book, and chapter 15 is the eight verses of preparation before it.

Another sign. The word is sēmeion, and John has used it twice before, both times in chapter 12 — the woman clothed with the sun (12:1) and the great red dragon (12:3). Those are the only three signs in the book. A woman, a dragon, and seven angels with the last plagues: the mother, the enemy, and the end.

Great and amazing is an odd pair of words for a plague, and John will use them again in three verses of God’s deeds. What is being described is not merely dreadful; it is astonishing, in the way something enormous and long-expected is astonishing when it finally begins.

And then the clause that governs the whole of chapter 16: which are the last, for with them the wrath of God is finished.

The verb is etelesthē — from teleō, to bring to an end, to complete. It is the same root as the word Jesus spoke from the cross: It is finished (John 19:30). Something is being brought to its appointed completion, and the sentence says so before a single bowl is lifted.

That is a strange and necessary thing to be told at this point in the book. A reader who has come through six chapters of dragons and beasts and marks might reasonably fear that the wrath of God is an inexhaustible reservoir with no bottom to it — that once it starts it simply continues. This verse says the opposite. The wrath of God has an end, and the end is in view from the moment it begins, and there is a last plague after which there are no more.

Which is not true of his mercy, and the contrast is the point. Scripture says his steadfast love endures for ever and never once says that of his anger. His anger is but for a moment, and his favour is for a lifetime (Ps. 30:5). He does not retain his anger for ever, because he delights in steadfast love (Mic. 7:18). Judgment in the Bible always has a stopping-point written into it; grace does not.

And there is one more thing in the word finished. If the wrath of God against sin is a thing that can be completed, then the question worth asking is where it was completed for a Christian — and the answer is the cross, where the same verb was used by the same author about the same event. There are two places in this book where God’s wrath is brought to its end. One of them is a hill outside Jerusalem, and it happened before any of this began.

verseByVerse.quote: And I saw what appeared to be a sea of glass mingled with fire—and also those who had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name, standing beside the sea of glass with harps of God in their hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I saw what appeared to be a sea of glass mingled with fire.

The sea of glass was there in chapter 4, stretched out in front of the throne, flat and still and transparent — chaos frozen solid under God’s feet (4:6). Now there is fire in it. Something has changed in the eleven chapters between, and the fire is judgment: the same fire that was taken from the altar and thrown down on the earth (8:5). The floor of heaven has begun to glow.

And also those who had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name, standing beside the sea of glass with harps of God in their hands.

Stop at the verb, because it directly contradicts something the reader was told two chapters ago. At 13:7 the beast was allowed to make war on the saints and to conquer them. Here the same people had conquered the beast. Same verb, nikaō, opposite direction, about the same encounter.

Both statements are true, and holding them together is the single most important thing this book asks of a suffering Christian. From the street, the beast won: the believers were arrested, tried, and killed, and there is no version of events in which that did not happen. From the sea of glass, they won: they are standing, with instruments in their hands, and the beast is not in the room.

And 12:11 has already explained how a defeat becomes a victory: they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death. The winning was not survival. It was refusing to let go, and the losing of the life was part of the mechanism rather than a failure of it.

Note what they conquered, listed in three parts: the beast and its image and the number of its name. Not an army — a demand. They were not asked to defeat anything; they were asked not to bow to it, not to worship an image, and not to take a number that would have let them keep trading. Their whole victory consists of things they did not do.

Say that plainly to any Christian who suspects his own faithfulness is too passive to count. The company standing on the sea of glass with harps did not storm anything. They declined. They said no to a formality, repeatedly, at increasing cost, and heaven files that under conquered.

And standing beside the sea. The picture is Israel on the far shore of the Red Sea with the water behind them and Egypt at the bottom of it — which is exactly what the next verse makes explicit. The people who came through are standing on the far bank, and the first thing they do is sing.

verseByVerse.quote: And they sing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, "Great and amazing are your deeds, O Lord God the Almighty! Just and true are your ways, O King of the nations! Who will not fear, O Lord, and glorify your name? For you alone are holy. All nations will come and worship you, for your righteous acts have been revealed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they sing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb.

Not two songs — one. The grammar allows a single song called by two names, and the content proves it: what follows is sung by both companies at once, because there is only one deliverance and it has two chapters.

The song of Moses is Exodus 15, sung on the far side of the sea with Pharaoh’s army drowned behind them. That is why John has just put these people beside the sea. Israel came out of Egypt through water; these have come out of the beast’s empire through fire and death; and the song is the same song, because the God who did the first did the second.

Then something surprising. The words that follow are not from Exodus 15 at all. They are a mosaic of the Psalms and the prophets, stitched together: Great and amazing are your deeds (Ps. 111:2); Just and true are your ways (Deut. 32:4); Who will not fear you, O King of the nations? (Jer. 10:7); All the nations you have made shall come and worship before you, O Lord, and shall glorify your name (Ps. 86:9). The redeemed of heaven sing in quotations. Their worship is made out of the Scriptures they were given, which is a quiet argument for filling a mind with them now.

And look at what the song is about, because it is not what a persecuted church would have been expected to sing. There is not one word in it about the beast, about the persecution, about what they suffered, or about their own endurance. Four clauses, and every one of them is about God: his deeds, his ways, his name, his righteous acts.

Just and true are your ways, O King of the nations! That is the sentence these particular singers are qualified to say. Anybody can affirm the justice of God from a comfortable chair. These people were killed for refusing a number, and they have come out the other side, and the first thing they say about the way God ran history is that it was just. No complaint. No question. Not because the question was never asked — it was, loudly, under the altar in 6:10 — but because it has been answered.

Who will not fear, O Lord, and glorify your name? For you alone are holy. The question is rhetorical and it expects the answer nobody. And the ground given is not power but holiness — the word sung three times by the living creatures in chapter 4. You alone: there is one of him, and the beast that demanded worship for forty-two months is not in the category.

All nations will come and worship you, for your righteous acts have been revealed. This is the widest sentence in the chapter, and it is startling in a book so full of judgment. The nations — who raged (11:18), who drank Babylon’s wine (14:8), over whom the beast was given authority (13:7) — will come and worship. It is Psalm 86:9 quoted straight, and it is the promise made to Abraham that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed.

This is not universalism; the same book that says this says that some are finally outside (21:8; 22:15). It is the assurance that the multitude of chapter 7 — from every nation and tribe and people and language — is not a consolation prize. God will have the nations. And the reason given is your righteous acts have been revealed: what finally brings the world in is not that God overwhelmed it, but that he was seen clearly.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–8 — The Sanctuary Filled with Smoke
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 5: the sanctuary of the tent of witness in heaven was opened. The phrase is the Old Testament’s name for the tabernacle, the tent that housed the ark, which housed the tablets called the testimony because they are God’s witness against a people who agreed to keep them (Ex. 38:21; Num. 1:50). The bowls come out of the place where the covenant is kept.

Verse 6: out come the seven angels, clothed in pure, bright linen, with golden sashes around their chests — priestly dress (Lev. 16:4; Dan. 10:5), and precisely how the risen Christ was described at 1:13.

Verse 7: one of the four living creatures — the beings nearest the throne, who never cease to say holy, holy, holy — hands over seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God. The word is phialē, a shallow libation dish that empties in a moment, not a jug.

Verse 8: the sanctuary was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from his power, and no one could enter the sanctuary until the seven plagues of the seven angels were finished.
verseByVerse.theology:
Judgment as Liturgy

The angels are dressed as priests, come out of a sanctuary, and are handed their vessels by a worshipper. That combination refuses two easy pictures at once: these are not demons let loose, and they are not soldiers. The judgment of God is not a loss of control and it is not outsourced. And the linen is pure and bright — the second word is used of the Bride’s dress at 19:8. Whatever a reader has to say about the severity of chapter 16, he will not be able to say that the hands carrying it were dirty.

The Same Golden Bowls

At 5:8 the elders held golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints. Here the same vessels, in the same throne room, are full of wrath. Golden bowls went up full of prayer; golden bowls come down full of judgment. The martyrs asked how long? and this is the crockery in which the answer is delivered. And the shape of the vessel is itself an argument: a trumpet is a warning, blown to be heard, giving time to respond; a libation bowl is tipped once and it is gone.

Smoke That Means Something Colder

Smoke filling the sanctuary is an old and glorious sight. When the tabernacle was finished the glory filled it and Moses could not enter (Ex. 40:34–35); at the dedication of the temple the priests could not stand to minister (1 Kings 8:10–11); Isaiah saw the house filled with smoke and cried Woe is me (Isa. 6:4–5). In every case the exclusion was temporary and joyful, and meant that God had come to dwell. Here it means that for the duration of the bowls, nobody goes in — and a sanctuary is where a priest goes in to intercede.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Bowls of wrath coming out of the tent of witness is not incidental. What is coming has a legal basis, and the document it rests on has been in the same box since Sinai. That is the difference between the judgments of this book and mere destruction.

Now: The most sobering sentence in the chapter is v. 8, and it should not be softened. There is no intercession while the bowls are being poured, because the time for it has run out. There comes a point at which the door is shut — not because God has become unwilling to hear, but because the case has been closed, the warnings have been given, and the answering has begun.

But note the exact wording, because the mercy is in it too: until. The closure has a limit, and it is the same limit given in v. 1 — the wrath of God is finished. Even the shutting of the sanctuary has an end date.

And the plain application, for anyone reading while the door is still open, is not complicated. It is open now. The sanctuary stands wide, and there is a great high priest inside it who always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Heb. 7:25). While that is true, pray — for yourself, and for the people whose names you would not want read out on the day the smoke fills the room.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I looked, and the sanctuary of the tent of witness in heaven was opened, and out of the sanctuary came the seven angels with the seven plagues, clothed in pure, bright linen, with golden sashes around their chests.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this I looked, and the sanctuary of the tent of witness in heaven was opened.

The phrase the tent of witness is precise and old. It is what the tabernacle is called in Exodus and Numbers — the tent that housed the ark, and the ark housed the two tablets of the law, which are called the testimony because they are God’s witness against a people who agreed to keep them and did not (Ex. 38:21; Num. 1:50).

So the bowls of wrath come out of the place where the covenant is kept. Not out of an armoury and not out of a prison, but out of the tent containing the terms both sides signed. That is the difference between the judgments of this book and mere destruction. What is coming has a legal basis, and the document it rests on has been in the same box since Sinai.

And it was opened. At 11:19 the temple in heaven was opened and the ark was seen; here the sanctuary opens again and something comes out of it. Twice in five chapters the doors of heaven’s holy place stand open, and the second time it is not to show the reader something but to release seven angels.

And out of the sanctuary came the seven angels with the seven plagues, clothed in pure, bright linen, with golden sashes around their chests.

They are dressed as priests. Linen was what the priest wore into the holy place (Lev. 16:4), and Daniel’s heavenly man was clothed in linen, with a belt of fine gold from Uphaz (Dan. 10:5). More pointedly still, a golden sash across the chest is exactly how the risen Christ was dressed in the first chapter of this book (1:13).

That combination should stop a reader, because it refuses two easy pictures at once. These are not demons let loose, and they are not soldiers. They are ministers in priestly dress, coming out of a sanctuary, carrying out a service. The judgment of God is not a loss of control and it is not an outsourcing; it is liturgy.

And the linen is pure and bright — the second word is the one used of the Bride’s dress at 19:8. Nothing that comes out of that door is dirty. Whatever a reader has to say about the severity of chapter 16, he will not be able to say that the hands carrying it were.

verseByVerse.quote: And one of the four living creatures gave to the seven angels seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God who lives forever and ever, and the sanctuary was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from his power, and no one could enter the sanctuary until the seven plagues of the seven angels were finished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And one of the four living creatures gave to the seven angels seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God who lives forever and ever.

The handover is made by one of the four living creatures — the beings nearest the throne, covered in eyes, who have been saying holy, holy, holy without ceasing since before the world was made (4:8). The worshippers are the ones who pass the bowls. Nothing in this chapter allows judgment to be handled by anybody outside the worship of God.

And the word for bowl is phialē — a shallow, wide dish used for pouring out a libation, not a jug or a jar. It empties in a moment. Compare the trumpets: a trumpet is a warning, blown to be heard, giving time to respond. A libation bowl is tipped once, and it is gone. The instrument itself says that the era of warnings is over.

The reader has seen golden bowls in this book before, and the connection is deliberate and almost unbearable. At 5:8 the elders held golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints. The same vessels, in the same throne room. Golden bowls went up full of prayer; golden bowls come down full of wrath. The martyrs asked how long? and this is the crockery in which the answer is delivered.

And the sanctuary was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from his power, and no one could enter the sanctuary until the seven plagues of the seven angels were finished.

Smoke filling the sanctuary is an old and glorious sight. When the tabernacle was finished, the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle. And Moses was not able to enter (Ex. 40:34–35). When Solomon dedicated the temple, the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud, for the glory of the LORD filled the house of God (1 Kings 8:10–11). Isaiah saw the house filled with smoke and cried Woe is me (Isa. 6:4–5).

In every one of those cases the smoke meant God had come to dwell, and the exclusion was temporary and joyful. Here it means something colder. No one could enter… until the seven plagues were finished.

Consider what the sanctuary is for. It is where a priest goes in to intercede. It is where blood is brought and pleading is done and mercy is asked for somebody else. And for the duration of the seven bowls, nobody goes in. There is no intercession while the plagues are being poured, because the time for it has run out.

That is the most sobering sentence in the chapter and it should not be softened. There comes a point at which the door is shut — not because God has become unwilling to hear, but because the case has been closed, the warnings have been given, and the answering has begun.

But note the exact wording, because it is also the mercy in the verse: until. The closure has a limit, and the limit is the same one given in verse 1 — the wrath of God is finished. Even the shutting of the sanctuary has an end date.

And the plain application, for anyone reading this while the door is still open, is not complicated. It is open now. The sanctuary is standing wide, and there is a great high priest inside it who always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Heb. 7:25). While that is true, pray — for yourself, and for the people whose names you would not want read out on the day the smoke fills the room.

15.text: <sup>1</sup>Then I saw another sign in heaven, great and amazing, seven angels with seven plagues, which are the last, for with them the wrath of God is finished.<sup>2</sup>And I saw what appeared to be a sea of glass mingled with fire—and also those who had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name, standing beside the sea of glass with harps of God in their hands.<sup>3</sup>And they sing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, “Great and amazing are your deeds, O Lord God the Almighty! Just and true are your ways, O King of the nations!<sup>4</sup>Who will not fear, O Lord, and glorify your name? For you alone are holy. All nations will come and worship you, for your righteous acts have been revealed.”<sup>5</sup>After this I looked, and the sanctuary of the tent of witness in heaven was opened,<sup>6</sup>and out of the sanctuary came the seven angels with the seven plagues, clothed in pure, bright linen, with golden sashes around their chests.<sup>7</sup>And one of the four living creatures gave to the seven angels seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God who lives forever and ever,<sup>8</sup>and the sanctuary was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from his power, and no one could enter the sanctuary until the seven plagues of the seven angels were finished.

16.title: The Seven Bowls: The Completion of Divine Justice
16.overview:
Chapter 16 is the third and final series of seven judgments in Revelation, and it is the most intense. Where the seals affected a quarter of the earth and the trumpets a third, the bowls are poured on the whole earth without fraction. The escalation is deliberate: the time for partial warning has passed. These are the last plagues, and with them the response of God to the accumulated rebellion of history reaches its completion.

The bowl series follows the Exodus plague pattern more closely than either the seals or the trumpets. Bowls one through five track the Egyptian plagues almost sequentially: sores (bowl 1, cf. Exodus 9:8–11), water turned to blood (bowls 2–3, cf. Exodus 7:17–21), darkness (bowl 5, cf. Exodus 10:21–23). The Exodus pattern is not decorative. It carries a theological message: the God who liberated Israel from Egypt is the same God who now acts in the final Exodus. The pattern of redemptive history repeats at the cosmic scale.

The chapter reaches its climax at the seventh bowl: a loud voice from the throne declares ‘It is done!’ and the greatest earthquake in human history splits the great city into three parts. Babylon is remembered before God and given the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath. Every island flees, every mountain disappears. The chapter ends not with despair but with the certainty that the one who declared ‘It is done’ from the cross has declared it again from the throne — all things are now moving irresistibly toward the new creation of chapters 21–22.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 1: a loud voice from the temple — almost certainly God’s own, since 15:8 has just closed the sanctuary to everyone else — orders the seven angels to pour. Verse 2: the first bowl brings harmful and painful sores on those who bore the mark of the beast and worshipped its image (cf. Ex. 9:8–11).

Verse 3: the sea becomes like the blood of a corpse and everything in it dies — against the second trumpet, which killed a third (8:8–9). Verse 4: the rivers and springs become blood, as the Nile did (Ex. 7:20–21).

Verses 5–7 stop the sequence and defend it. The angel in charge of the waters — whose department has just been ruined — declares Just are you, O Holy One… they have shed the blood of saints and prophets, and you have given them blood to drink. It is what they deserve! And then the altar itself answers: Yes, Lord God the Almighty, true and just are your judgments!

Verses 8–9: the fourth bowl turns the sun up, and they cursed the name of God who had power over these plagues. They did not repent and give him glory. Verses 10–11: the fifth falls on the throne of the beast and its kingdom goes dark (cf. Ex. 10:21–23); people gnaw their tongues in anguish and curse the God of heaven for their pain and sores, and did not repent of their deeds.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Same Ground, Undiluted

The bowls strike the same targets as the trumpets in the same order — earth, sea, rivers and springs, sun, darkness on a kingdom, the Euphrates, and a final convulsion with hail (cf. 8:7–12; 9:13–14). What changes is the extent: the trumpets took a third, the bowls take everything. That parallel is one of the strongest arguments for reading the three sevens as recapitulation, the same ground covered again at greater intensity. And five of the ten plagues of Egypt are in this one chapter — sores, water to blood, darkness, frogs and hail.

The Theodicy of the Book

Verses 5–7 are where Revelation stops and answers the question a reader has carried since chapter 6: is this fair? The answer is not argued by John but sung, in the middle of the plague, by the angel with most cause to object. The grounds are the oldest principle of justice there is — the punishment is the crime, served back. And note who is not saying it is what they deserve: no human being in this book ever pronounces that sentence over another. Vengeance is God’s alone because only he can be trusted to get it exactly right (Rom. 12:19).

Then the altar speaks, and John lets the strange sentence stand. Under that altar are the souls who cried how long before you will judge and avenge our blood? (6:9–10). This is the altar answering its own question, and the verdict of the people who actually paid for the injustice is yes — not at last, not it took long enough. Nobody in heaven, seeing the whole file, thinks God has overdone it.

Judgment Fits the Offence

The bowls are not indiscriminate. The sores fall on the people who bore the mark — what was taken as a passport to buying and selling turns out to be the wound. God rarely invents a punishment unconnected to the offence; he hands people over to what they insisted on having (Rom. 1:24, 26, 28).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: To darken an empire was to judge its god. Egypt worshipped the sun and Pharaoh claimed to be his son, and the ninth plague showed that the chief god of the empire could not keep his own lamp lit. Every empire demanding worship rests on an appearance of permanence — the lights are on, the courts sit, the coins are minted. One bowl on the throne of the beast, and the kingdom is in the dark.

Now: Three times in this chapter John records that people cursed God and did not repent, and v. 9 contains the extraordinary detail: they curse the name of God who had power over these plagues. They know. There is no ignorance here and no confusion about the source. Suffering has not hidden God from them; it has revealed him, and they have decided against him with the evidence in front of them.

The warning in that is not chiefly about other people. Every Christian meets small versions of it: the illness, the loss, the disappointment that could go either way. Two men lose the same thing in the same week and one is driven to his knees while the other never prays again, and the difference is not the weight of the trouble. It is which way a person was already facing when it landed.

And notice what they curse God for: for their pain and sores. The entire content of their complaint is their own discomfort. So here is a test worth running before the fifth bowl rather than after it. When you last had a grievance against God, what was it actually about? If the honest answer is that he had not arranged your comfort as you would have arranged it, that is the identical complaint at a survivable scale — and there is still time to say so.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I heard a loud voice from the temple telling the seven angels, "Go and pour out on the earth the seven bowls of the wrath of God." So the first angel went and poured out his bowl on the earth, and harmful and painful sores came upon the people who bore the mark of the beast and worshiped its image.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I heard a loud voice from the temple telling the seven angels, “Go and pour out on the earth the seven bowls of the wrath of God.”

Nobody in the previous chapter could enter the sanctuary, and the voice comes out of it anyway. It is almost certainly God’s own; 15:8 has just said the temple is full of the smoke of his glory and closed to everybody else. Whoever else is involved in what follows, the order to begin is given by the one on the throne.

Before the first bowl is tipped, three things about this chapter should be set out, because they govern all twenty-one verses.

First, the targets are the same as the trumpets, in the same order: the earth, the sea, the rivers and springs, the sun, darkness on a kingdom, the Euphrates, and a final convulsion with hail. Compare 8:7–12 and 9:13–14 and the correspondence is almost item for item. What has changed is the extent. The trumpets struck a third; the bowls strike everything. That parallel is one of the strongest arguments for reading the three sevens as recapitulation — the same ground covered again at greater intensity — and it is why the question was set out at 6:1 rather than left to the reader.

Second, the plagues of Egypt are here again, and more densely than anywhere else in the book: sores (Ex. 9:10), water to blood (Ex. 7:20), darkness (Ex. 10:22), frogs (Ex. 8:6) and hail (Ex. 9:24). Five of the ten, in one chapter. The empire is Egypt and the God who broke Egypt has not changed his methods.

Third, and this is the drumbeat of the chapter: three times John will record that the people struck by these plagues cursed God and did not repent (vv. 9, 11, 21).

So the first angel went and poured out his bowl on the earth, and harmful and painful sores came upon the people who bore the mark of the beast and worshiped its image.

The sixth plague on Egypt was boils breaking out in sores on man and beast (Ex. 9:8–11), and it is the one the magicians could not stand up to: they could not stand before Moses because the boils were on them too. Whatever else Egypt’s wisdom could imitate, it could not imitate health.

And note precisely who is struck: the people who bore the mark of the beast and worshiped its image. The bowls are not indiscriminate. Chapter 13 said that anyone who refused the mark could not buy or sell — the mark was the ticket to a working life. Here the mark itself festers. What was taken as a passport turns out to be the wound.

State that plainly, because it removes the sense of arbitrariness. That is how judgment usually works in Scripture. God rarely invents a punishment unconnected to the offence. He hands people over to what they insisted on having — God gave them up, three times in one paragraph (Rom. 1:24, 26, 28). The sore appears exactly where the mark was.

verseByVerse.quote: The second angel poured out his bowl into the sea, and it became like the blood of a corpse, and every living thing died that was in the sea. The third angel poured out his bowl into the rivers and the springs of water, and they became blood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second angel poured out his bowl into the sea, and it became like the blood of a corpse, and every living thing died that was in the sea.

The comparison is deliberately revolting, and the ESV keeps it: not bright arterial blood but the blood of a corpse — dark, thickened, going bad. Anyone who has been in a room with a body knows what is being described.

And set it against the second trumpet, which turned a third of the sea to blood and killed a third of the creatures in it (8:8–9). Here there is no fraction. Every living thing died that was in the sea. The restraint that has governed every judgment in this book since chapter 6 — a fourth, a third, a tenth, forty-two months, a fence around the winds — is gone. This is what 15:1 meant by the wrath of God being poured out undiluted.

The third angel poured out his bowl into the rivers and the springs of water, and they became blood.

The first plague on Egypt turned the Nile to blood so that the fish died and the river stank and the Egyptians could not drink from it (Ex. 7:20–21). And the reason for that plague is stated in the chapter before: Pharaoh had ordered every Hebrew boy thrown into that river. The Nile was given back to Egypt in the condition Egypt had put it in.

Take the two bowls together and notice what has been removed. The sea is where the beast came from (13:1) and where the world’s trade ran; the rivers and springs are where a settlement gets its drinking water. Between them they are everything wet on the planet — commerce and survival — and both are now blood. In one stroke the world has lost what it lives on and what it lives by.

And the springs have been touched once before. At the third trumpet a star called Wormwood fell on the rivers and the springs of water and made a third of them bitter, and many died (8:10–11). Bitter water can still be drunk by a desperate man. Blood cannot. The trumpet made the water unbearable; the bowl makes it impossible, and the distance between the two is the distance between a warning and a verdict.

There is a plain and uncomfortable observation to be made about the created order here, and it runs through the whole book. Everything the world depends on belongs to somebody. The sea a merchant sails on, the spring a village was built around, the sun a farmer plants by — none of it is neutral machinery that happens to be reliable. It is being upheld, moment by moment, by the one who is being cursed for withdrawing it. A civilisation can spend centuries assuming the water will be there, and be right every single day, and still be wrong about why.

And then John does something at this point that he does nowhere else in the bowl sequence. He stops. The fourth bowl does not follow the third; three verses of worship follow it instead, because heaven has something to say about whether this is fair.

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard the angel in charge of the waters say, "Just are you, O Holy One, who is and who was, for you brought these judgments. For they have shed the blood of saints and prophets, and you have given them blood to drink. It is what they deserve!" And I heard the altar saying, "Yes, Lord God the Almighty, true and just are your judgments!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I heard the angel in charge of the waters say, “Just are you, O Holy One, who is and who was, for you brought these judgments. For they have shed the blood of saints and prophets, and you have given them blood to drink. It is what they deserve!”

These three verses are the theodicy of the book — the place where Revelation stops and answers the question a reader has been carrying since chapter 6. Is this fair? And the answer is not given by John, or by an apostle, or by an argument. It is sung, in the middle of the plague, by the angel whose department has just been ruined.

That detail should not be missed. The angel in charge of the waters is the one who has just watched every river and spring under his care turn to blood. If anybody in the universe had grounds to file an objection, it is him. He declares the judgment just.

The grounds are stated in one sentence, and it is the oldest principle of justice there is: they have shed the blood of saints and prophets, and you have given them blood to drink. The punishment is the crime, served back. Egypt drowned Hebrew children in a river and had to drink the river. These people made the earth run with the blood of the saints, and now there is nothing else to drink. Nothing arbitrary is being done. What God does to the wicked is what the wicked did, returned.

It is what they deserve. Three words in English and two in Greek, and they are not comfortable. But notice who is not saying them: no human being in this book ever pronounces that sentence over another. The martyrs under the altar asked how long? and left the verdict to God (6:10). Vengeance is God’s and the reason it is his alone is that only he can be trusted to get it exactly right (Rom. 12:19).

And the title used of God here is chosen with care: O Holy One, who is and who was. The threefold name has lost its third term again, as at 11:17 — the one who is to come has come — and the attribute picked out is holy. Not powerful. The angel is not saying God has the right to do this because he is strong enough. He is saying it is consistent with what God is.

And I heard the altar saying, “Yes, Lord God the Almighty, true and just are your judgments!”

The altar speaks. It is a strange sentence and John lets it stand, and any reader who has been following will know why the furniture is given a voice. Under that altar are the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God, who cried O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood? (6:9–10). They were given white robes and told to rest a little longer.

This is the altar answering its own question. The same two words come back — holy and true there, true and just here — and the verdict of the people who actually paid for the injustice is yes. Not at last, and not it took long enough. Yes.

Which is the most important thing this chapter has to say to a Christian who finds these plagues hard to look at, and it should be taken seriously. The one group whose opinion might be thought to carry most weight — the murdered, who wanted this and waited for it — are the ones who declare it just when it comes. Nobody in heaven, seeing the whole file, thinks God has overdone it.

verseByVerse.quote: The fourth angel poured out his bowl on the sun, and it was allowed to scorch people with fire. They were scorched by the fierce heat, and they cursed the name of God who had power over these plagues. They did not repent and give him glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fourth angel poured out his bowl on the sun, and it was allowed to scorch people with fire. They were scorched by the fierce heat, and they cursed the name of God who had power over these plagues. They did not repent and give him glory.

It was allowed. Even here, at full strength, with the limits off the extent of the judgment, the divine passive holds. Nothing in this book acts on its own authority, and the sun is no exception.

The fourth trumpet darkened a third of the sun (8:12); the fourth bowl turns it up. And the reversal is pointed, because the great promise made to the multitude in 7:16 was the sun shall not strike them, nor any scorching heat. Two companies, one sun. For the sealed it is shaded by the tent of God spread over them; for these it is a furnace. The same created thing behaves differently depending on whose you are.

Then the sentence that is repeated three times in this chapter, and it is the most sobering diagnosis in the New Testament: they cursed the name of God… They did not repent and give him glory.

Three things are packed into it.

They cursed. The word is blasphēmeō — the same verb used of the beast’s mouth in 13:6. Under the plague they have started to sound like the thing they worshipped.

They cursed the name of God who had power over these plagues. This is the extraordinary part. They know. There is no ignorance here, no confusion about the source, no atheism. They have correctly identified who is doing this and they curse him for it. Suffering has not hidden God from them; it has revealed him, and they have decided against him with the evidence in front of them.

And they did not repent and give him glory. Which is the answer, given for the third time in this book, to a hope that most people carry quietly: that if things got bad enough, people would turn. Chapter 9 said it after a third of mankind died. Chapter 16 says it three times more. Pain does not produce repentance. It reveals what was already there, and it hardens as reliably as it softens.

There is a warning in that for a believer, and it is not the obvious one. It is not chiefly a warning about other people. Every Christian meets small versions of this: the illness, the loss, the disappointment that could go either way — and the direction it goes is not decided by the size of the trouble. Two men lose the same thing in the same week, and one is driven to his knees and the other never prays again. The difference is not the weight. It is which direction a person was already facing when it landed.

And note what repentance is called here: repent and give him glory. Not repent and feel sorry. To repent is to hand God back the glory that was given to something else — which is precisely what these people will not do, because they gave it to a beast and they are not taking it back.

verseByVerse.quote: The fifth angel poured out his bowl on the throne of the beast, and its kingdom was plunged into darkness. People gnawed their tongues in anguish and cursed the God of heaven for their pain and sores. They did not repent of their deeds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fifth angel poured out his bowl on the throne of the beast, and its kingdom was plunged into darkness.

The first four bowls fell on creation — earth, sea, rivers, sun. The fifth falls on a government. And it is aimed with precision: not at the beast’s subjects, or its armies, but at the throne of the beast, the seat of the thing itself. The reader last heard about a throne in Pergamum, where Satan’s throne is (2:13). Christians had been living under its shadow for the whole book. It goes dark.

The ninth plague on Egypt was a darkness that could be felt, three days in which nobody rose from his place — but all the people of Israel had light where they lived (Ex. 10:21–23). And the god being judged was the sun, the head of the Egyptian pantheon, whose son Pharaoh claimed to be. To darken the empire is to show that its god cannot keep a lamp lit.

Which is what makes the fifth bowl different from the four before it. The others damaged the world; this one exposes the regime. Every empire that demands worship rests on an appearance of permanence — the lights are on, the courts sit, the coins are minted, and it is inconceivable that any of it should stop. One bowl, and the kingdom is in the dark. It could not even manage light.

People gnawed their tongues in anguish and cursed the God of heaven for their pain and sores. They did not repent of their deeds.

Gnawing the tongue is a small, physical, entirely credible detail — what a person does with pain he cannot get away from and cannot cry out about usefully. And the sores are the ones from the first bowl, still there. The plagues in this chapter accumulate; nothing has healed.

And then the refrain for the second time, with one word changed. In verse 9 they did not repent and give him glory. Here they did not repent of their deeds. The first is about worship, the second about behaviour, and together they cover the ground: they will not change what they adore and they will not change what they do.

Notice, too, what they curse God for: for their pain and sores. Not for anything they have thought about, and not for any account of who he is. The entire content of their complaint is their own discomfort. It is possible to spend a life measuring God exclusively by how one feels, and this is what that comes to in the end.

Which suggests a test worth running before the fifth bowl rather than after it. When you last found yourself with a grievance against God, what was it actually about? If the honest answer is that he had not arranged your comfort as you would have arranged it, that is the identical complaint, at a survivable scale, and there is still time to say so.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–21 — The Sixth and Seventh Bowls
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 12: the sixth bowl dries the Euphrates to prepare the way for the kings from the east — and when Cyrus took Babylon his engineers diverted that river and his troops walked in up the empty bed, exactly as Isaiah had said (Isa. 44:27–28). Verses 13–14: three unclean spirits like frogs (Ex. 8:6) come out of the mouths of the dragon, the beast and the false prophet — the unholy trinity together for the first time — and go to the kings of the world to assemble them for battle.

Verse 15 interrupts, in brackets, in Christ’s own voice: Behold, I am coming like a thief! Blessed is the one who stays awake, keeping his garments on, that he may not go about naked and be seen exposed! — the third of the book’s seven beatitudes. Verse 16 names the muster point: Armageddon, its only occurrence in the Bible.

Verse 17: the seventh bowl is poured into the air, and a loud voice from the temple and the throne says It is done! — gegonen, a perfect tense, the completion promised at 15:1. Verse 18: the storm signs at full strength, with an earthquake such as there had never been since man was on the earth.

Verse 19: the great city splits in three, the cities of the nations fall, and God remembered Babylon the great, to make her drain the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath. Verse 20: every island flees and no mountains are found (cf. 6:14). Verse 21: hailstones of about a hundred pounds fall (Ex. 9:24) — and they cursed God, for the third time in the chapter, which is the last thing humanity does in it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Whole Arsenal Is Rhetorical

The dragon, the beast and the false prophet appear together at last, and all three of them do the same thing: they speak. Three mouths, one output each. The dragon is the deceiver of the whole world (12:9); the beast was given a mouth uttering haughty words (13:5); the false prophet deceives by signs. The last war in this book begins not with a mobilisation but with a persuasion campaign — and the persuading is done by demons who look absurd and are believed anyway. Everything about these villains has been magnificent until now: seven heads, ten diadems, a healed wound, the worship of the whole earth. When their propaganda is finally shown, it hops.

Armageddon

An enormous popular literature rests on one verse, and honesty requires saying that its meaning is not certain. The likeliest derivation is har-Megiddon, the mountain of Megiddo — the fortress guarding the pass into Jezreel and the most fought-over place in the land (Judg. 5:19; 2 Kings 9:27; 23:29–30). The difficulty is that Megiddo is a mound on a plain, not a mountain; so some read mountain of assembly (Isa. 14:13), and others take it as a symbolic name for the final confrontation wherever it happens — which fits a book that has already called one city Sodom, Egypt and Babylon.

What is not uncertain is the outcome, or the length. The kings are assembled here and nothing happens; the fighting is described at 19:19–21, and it lasts one verse, and the weapon is a sword out of a mouth. Armageddon is the most famous battle in the world’s imagination and the shortest in the book.

“It Is Done”

This author uses that word three times, and the three are the frame of everything: on the cross, It is finished (John 19:30); here, the end of wrath; and at 21:6, of the new creation. What was accomplished at the first makes the second bearable and the third certain. And there is no eighth bowl.

“God Remembered Babylon”

In Scripture God remembering never means something had slipped his mind. It is covenant language and always means he is about to act on what he has long known: God remembered Noah, and the waters went down (Gen. 8:1); God remembered his covenant with Abraham, and the exodus began (Ex. 2:24). A file open since 14:8 has come to the top of the pile, and chapters 17 and 18 will do nothing else.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A Levite found asleep on watch in the temple had his clothes taken and burned, and was driven out naked in front of everyone. Being caught asleep meant being publicly undressed, and v. 15 would have made a Christian in Asia smile before it made him think. Garments in this book have a settled meaning: white robes for those who conquer (3:5), robes washed in the blood of the Lamb (7:14), the fine linen that is the righteous deeds of the saints (19:8) — and Laodicea was told to buy them so that the shame of your nakedness may not be seen (3:18), the same phrase.

Now: Verse 15 is the most striking pastoral moment in the chapter, and the interruption is itself the message. Christ has not spoken directly since chapter 3 and will not again until chapter 22; he breaks in here, mid-sentence, while demonic frogs are assembling the kings of the world — and his concern is one Christian staying awake and keeping his clothes on. The cosmic scale of this chapter never once displaces the person reading it. And what is asked is not heroic: not that a believer do anything about the coalition, but that he be found alert and dressed.

The earthquake of v. 18 is a sorting rather than demolition for its own sake. God said Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also the heavens (Hag. 2:6), and Hebrews draws out why: the removal of what can be shaken, in order that the things that cannot be shaken may remain (Heb. 12:26–28). The honest question on reading it is therefore not will I survive this? but how much of what I am currently leaning on is in the shakeable category?

And the chapter ends where it does on purpose. Revelation offers no consoling picture of a world that finally comes round under pressure; it has now said four times that judgment by itself changes nobody. What changes people is what happened at 11:13, where two witnesses were killed and raised and nine tenths of a city gave glory to God, and what was announced at 14:6. The bowls are the answer to how long? They are not the instrument of anybody’s salvation. That instrument has been standing in the middle of the throne since chapter 5, and while the door of the sanctuary is open it is still working.

verseByVerse.quote: The sixth angel poured out his bowl on the great river Euphrates, and its water was dried up, to prepare the way for the kings from the east. And I saw, coming out of the mouth of the dragon and out of the mouth of the beast and out of the mouth of the false prophet, three unclean spirits like frogs. For they are demonic spirits, performing signs, who go abroad to the kings of the whole world, to assemble them for battle on the great day of God the Almighty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sixth angel poured out his bowl on the great river Euphrates, and its water was dried up, to prepare the way for the kings from the east.

The Euphrates was the eastern frontier of the empire and the direction every invasion of Israel had come from, and the reader has been here before: at the sixth trumpet four angels were released who had been bound at this same river (9:14). Now the river itself goes.

A dried-up river is one of Scripture’s standard pictures of God clearing a road. He dried the Red Sea for Israel to walk through (Ex. 14:21) and the Jordan for them to enter the land (Josh. 3:16). And when Cyrus took Babylon, according to the ancient historians, his engineers diverted the Euphrates and his troops walked into the city up the empty riverbed — which is what Isaiah had prophesied when he named Cyrus and said God would dry up the deep (Isa. 44:27–28). A first-century reader hearing that the Euphrates had been dried for kings from the east knew exactly how the last great Babylon fell.

The irony is that the water is removed to make an invasion easier. God is not defending the beast’s kingdom; he is opening the gate for the thing that will destroy it. Even the enemies of God’s people serve his purposes without knowing it.

And I saw, coming out of the mouth of the dragon and out of the mouth of the beast and out of the mouth of the false prophet, three unclean spirits like frogs.

The unholy trinity of chapters 12 and 13 appears together for the first time, and notice what all three of them do. They speak. Three mouths, and one thing comes out of each. The dragon was called the deceiver of the whole world (12:9); the beast was given a mouth uttering haughty and blasphemous words (13:5); the false prophet deceives by signs. The entire arsenal of evil in this book is rhetorical.

And what comes out is like frogs, which is the second plague on Egypt (Ex. 8:6) — and, to a Jewish reader, unclean by law (Lev. 11:10–12). It is also, deliberately, ridiculous. Everything about this book’s villains has been magnificent so far: seven heads, ten diadems, a mortal wound healed, the worship of the whole earth. And when their propaganda is finally shown, it hops.

For they are demonic spirits, performing signs, who go abroad to the kings of the whole world, to assemble them for battle on the great day of God the Almighty.

The frogs are a diplomatic service. They go to the kings of the earth, they perform signs, and they assemble a coalition. This is how the last war begins in Revelation: not with a mobilisation but with a persuasion campaign, and the persuading is done by demons who look absurd and are believed anyway.

Set that beside the way people usually imagine spiritual warfare. The decisive struggle in this book is not fought with weapons and is not chiefly about power. It is about what the world is told and whether it believes it. The dragon’s one method, from a conversation in a garden to the last coalition on earth, is to say something untrue convincingly.

verseByVerse.quote: ("Behold, I am coming like a thief! Blessed is the one who stays awake, keeping his garments on, that he may not go about naked and be seen exposed!") And they assembled them at the place that in Hebrew is called Armageddon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And then, in the middle of a sentence about demonic frogs assembling the kings of the world, a different voice cuts in. The ESV marks it with brackets, and rightly.

(“Behold, I am coming like a thief! Blessed is the one who stays awake, keeping his garments on, that he may not go about naked and be seen exposed!”)

Christ interrupts his own book. He has not spoken directly since chapter 3, and he does not speak again until chapter 22 — and here, at the darkest point of the narrative, he breaks in without introduction to say two things to the reader.

The interruption is itself the message. The armies are gathering; the frogs are going out to the kings; the last battle is being assembled. And the Lord’s concern, at that exact moment, is a Christian in Thyatira staying awake and keeping his clothes on. The cosmic scale of this chapter never once displaces the person reading it.

I am coming like a thief. He said it to Sardis in the same words (3:3) and he said it in Galilee (Matt. 24:43), and Paul and Peter both repeat it (1 Thess. 5:2; 2 Pet. 3:10). The point of the image is never stealth — a thief does not sneak so much as arrive on a night nobody expected. It is unpredictability, and its practical consequence is that there is no point in a person planning to get ready later.

Blessed is the one who stays awake — the third of the book’s seven beatitudes. Keeping his garments on, that he may not go about naked and be seen exposed. The image would have made a Christian in Asia smile before it made him think. The captain of the temple guard in Jerusalem went round at night, and a Levite found asleep at his post had his clothes taken and burned, so that he was driven out of the temple naked in front of everybody. Being caught asleep meant being publicly undressed.

And garments in this book have a settled meaning: white robes given to those who conquer (3:5), robes washed and made white in the blood of the Lamb (7:14), the fine linen of the Bride which is the righteous deeds of the saints (19:8). And Laodicea was told to buy white garments so that the shame of your nakedness may not be seen (3:18) — the same phrase.

So the instruction is not complicated and it is not heroic. Stay awake. Keep your clothes on. That is what is asked of a Christian while the kings of the earth are being assembled for Armageddon: not that he do anything about the coalition, but that he be found alert and dressed.

And they assembled them at the place that in Hebrew is called Armageddon.

This is the only occurrence of the word in the Bible, and an enormous popular literature rests on one verse. Honesty requires saying that its meaning is not certain.

The likeliest derivation is har-Megiddon, the mountain of Megiddo. Megiddo was a fortress town guarding the pass into the plain of Jezreel, and it is the most fought-over place in the land: Deborah and Barak defeated Sisera at Taanach, by the waters of Megiddo (Judg. 5:19); Ahaziah died there (2 Kings 9:27); and good king Josiah was killed there by Pharaoh Neco, and all Judah mourned (2 Kings 23:29–30; 2 Chr. 35:22–25). To say Megiddo was to say the battlefield.

The difficulty is that Megiddo is a mound on a plain, not a mountain. Some therefore read mountain of assembly, the phrase Isaiah puts in the mouth of the fallen day-star who says I will sit on the mount of assembly in the far reaches of the north (Isa. 14:13). Others take it as a symbolic name for the final confrontation wherever it happens, which fits a book that has just told the reader that Sodom, Egypt and Babylon are all names for one city.

What is not uncertain is who wins, and how little of a battle it turns out to be. The kings are assembled here in chapter 16 and nothing happens; the fighting is described in 19:19–21, and it lasts one verse, and the weapon is a sword out of a mouth. Armageddon is the most famous battle in the world’s imagination and the shortest in the book.
