When I saw her, I marveled greatly.<sup>7</sup>But the angel said to me, “Why do you marvel? I will tell you the mystery of the woman, and of the beast with seven heads and ten horns that carries her.<sup>8</sup>The beast that you saw was, and is not, and is about to rise from the bottomless pit and go to destruction. And the dwellers on earth whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world will marvel to see the beast, because it was and is not and is to come.<sup>9</sup>This calls for a mind with wisdom: the seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman is seated;<sup>10</sup>they are also seven kings, five of whom have fallen, one is, the other has not yet come, and when he does come he must remain only a little while.<sup>11</sup>As for the beast that was and is not, it is an eighth but it belongs to the seven, and it goes to destruction.<sup>12</sup>And the ten horns that you saw are ten kings who have not yet received royal power, but they are to receive authority as kings for one hour, together with the beast.<sup>13</sup>These are of one mind, and they hand over their power and authority to the beast.<sup>14</sup>They will make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those with him are called and chosen and faithful.”<sup>15</sup>And the angel said to me, “The waters that you saw, where the prostitute is seated, are peoples and multitudes and nations and languages.<sup>16</sup>And the ten horns that you saw, they and the beast will hate the prostitute. They will make her desolate and naked, and devour her flesh and burn her up with fire,<sup>17</sup>for God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose by being of one mind and handing over their royal power to the beast, until the words of God are fulfilled.<sup>18</sup>And the woman that you saw is the great city that has dominion over the kings of the earth.”

18.title: Fallen, Fallen Is Babylon the Great
18.overview:
Chapter 18 is Revelation’s sustained lament over the fall of the great city. It is the longest single chapter in the book, and it is deliberately literary in character — structured like the great prophetic dirges of the Old Testament (Isaiah 13–14 over Babylon; Ezekiel 26–28 over Tyre; Ezekiel 27 especially, whose cargo list John adapts in vv. 12–13). The chapter uses the Old Testament’s own poetic forms to announce the end of the Old Testament’s great enemy.

The chapter moves through three distinct movements. First (vv. 1–8): the angelic announcement of Babylon’s fall and the call for God’s people to come out of her. Second (vv. 9–20): the threefold lament of the kings, merchants, and seafarers — three groups whose wealth depended on Babylon, each mourning from a safe distance as the city burns. Third (vv. 21–24): the millstone sign and the sevenfold silence — the total, irreversible end of the city that made the nations drunk with her wine.

The economic detail of chapter 18 is one of its most striking features. The cargo list of vv. 12–13 is specific, comprehensive, and damning — ending with ‘slaves, that is, human souls.’ Babylon’s economy is built on everything, including people. The city that offered the nations luxury and culture and wealth was also the city that traded in human beings as commodities. This is Revelation’s most direct indictment of the economics of empire, and it is not limited to the Roman slave trade: every economic system that treats human beings as means rather than ends falls under the same indictment.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Announcement and the Call
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 1: an angel with great authority comes down and the earth was made bright with his glory (cf. Ezek. 43:2). Verses 2–3: Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great! — the announcement of 14:8 now given twenty-four verses instead of one. She becomes a haunt of demons and unclean birds, which is exactly what the prophets said of the first Babylon (Isa. 13:21–22; Jer. 50:39). And three groups are named who will structure the chapter: the nations who drank, the kings who traded, and — new here — the merchants, who grew rich from the power of her luxurious living.

Verses 4–5: Come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues (Jer. 51:45; Isa. 52:11; cf. 2 Cor. 6:17), for her sins are heaped high as heaven — a tower again (Gen. 11:4) — and God has remembered her iniquities.

Verses 6–8: repay her double in the cup she mixed; and Babylon speaks in her own voice, quoted from Isaiah’s taunt against the original city (Isa. 47:7–8): I sit as a queen, I am no widow, and mourning I shall never see. The three things she says she will never see are the three that arrive: death and mourning and famine, all in a single day.
verseByVerse.theology:
Chapter 17 and Chapter 18 Are the Same City

Chapter 17 showed Babylon as a religious and political power — a prostitute demanding worship, riding a beast, drunk on the blood of the saints. Chapter 18 shows her as an economy, and the charge sheet is a cargo manifest. That is the point: what the beast enforces by law, Babylon sustains by trade. And v. 3 names the mechanism exactly — her hold on the merchants was not that she threatened them but that she made them rich.

“Come Out of Her” Is Not Emigration

It cannot mean physical withdrawal, and the New Testament settles that: Christians stayed in Rome; Jesus prayed not that you take them out of the world (John 17:15); Paul said avoiding immoral people altogether would mean leaving the world entirely (1 Cor. 5:9–10). The verse says what it means, in two parallel clauses: lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues. It is non-participation — living in the city, working in it, paying for it, praying for it, and not joining in what it does or wanting what it wants.

Which is harder than moving house. Nobody has to decide whether to leave a country; everybody has to decide, repeatedly and in small instalments, whether to make the arrangement everyone makes. Coming out of Babylon happens on Tuesday afternoons, and nobody photographs it.

Is “Double” Unjust?

The Hebrew idiom behind it answers the question. Mishneh is used of a garment folded so that the two halves match exactly — the second is not extra but corresponding — and Isaiah promised Israel a double that plainly meant full compensation (Isa. 40:2; 61:7). The rest of the sentence makes it explicit: mix a double portion for her in the cup she mixed. Her own cup, her own recipe, folded back. Nothing new has been added. And note that no Christian in this book repays anybody; 17:16 has already said the beast and the ten kings destroy her.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Verse 2 is a ruin at night. The great houses are still standing and the streets are still laid out, and what moves in them are owls and jackals. Anyone who has walked through an abandoned town knows the effect — the buildings are what make it terrible, because they were built for people and there are no people. The word translated haunt is literally a prison: the city that offered the world its freedom has become a cage for unclean things.

Now: Babylon’s boast in v. 7 is not principally arrogance, and that is why a comfortable church finds this chapter hard to feel. The claim is not I am better than others; it is this will go on. Three denials of something ordinary: permanent authority, nothing she depends on can die, and she is exempt from grief. Anyone who has never seriously reckoned with the possibility that his country, his savings, his health or his arrangements might simply stop has said that sentence in his heart without ever putting it into words.

And Laodicea said the same thing in different vocabulary — I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing (3:17) — which is the warning that it can be said inside a church as easily as inside an empire. Her sins are stacked to heaven, which is where Babylon always wanted to reach, and it is her record that arrived.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I saw another angel coming down from heaven, having great authority, and the earth was made bright with his glory. And he called out with a mighty voice, "Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great! She has become a dwelling place for demons, a haunt for every unclean spirit, a haunt for every unclean bird, a haunt for every unclean and detestable beast. For all nations have drunk the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality, and the kings of the earth have committed immorality with her, and the merchants of the earth have grown rich from the power of her luxurious living."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this I saw another angel coming down from heaven, having great authority, and the earth was made bright with his glory.

The detail is easy to miss and it sets the tone of the chapter. This angel is bright enough that the whole earth lights up as he descends. Ezekiel saw the same thing when the glory of God returned to the temple — the earth shone with his glory (Ezek. 43:2). The city about to be described as the most magnificent in the world is about to be lit by something that makes it look like a candle at noon.

And he called out with a mighty voice, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!” The announcement made in one verse at 14:8 is now made again, and this time the chapter does not move on. Twenty-four verses of it. And the words are still Isaiah’s watchman on the wall (Isa. 21:9).

She has become a dwelling place for demons, a haunt for every unclean spirit, a haunt for every unclean bird, a haunt for every unclean and detestable beast.

This is exactly what the prophets said would happen to the first Babylon, and John is quoting deliberately. Isaiah: wild animals will lie down there, and their houses will be full of howling creatures… hyenas will cry in its towers, and jackals in the pleasant palaces (Isa. 13:21–22). Jeremiah said the same of Babylon (Jer. 50:39) and of Edom.

Consider what that means as a picture. It is a ruin at night. The great houses are still standing; the streets are still laid out; and what moves in them are owls and jackals. Anyone who has walked through an abandoned town knows the effect — the buildings are what make it terrible, because they were built for people and there are no people.

And the word haunt is literally a prison or a place of keeping. The city that offered the whole world its freedom has become a cage for unclean things.

For all nations have drunk the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality, and the kings of the earth have committed immorality with her, and the merchants of the earth have grown rich from the power of her luxurious living.

Three groups, and this verse is the chapter’s table of contents. The kings will lament in verses 9 and 10, the merchants in 11 to 16, and the seafarers in 17 to 19. But notice the third group, because it is new. In chapter 17 the parties to Babylon’s business were the kings and the drunken populace. Here the merchants arrive, and from verse 11 onward they will dominate the chapter.

That shift is the most striking thing about these two chapters read together. Chapter 17 showed Babylon as a religious and political power — a prostitute demanding worship, riding a beast, drunk on the blood of the saints. Chapter 18 shows her as an economy. The charge sheet is a cargo manifest. And it turns out the two are the same city, which is the point: what the beast enforces by law, Babylon sustains by trade.

And the last phrase names the mechanism precisely: the power of her luxurious living. The Greek word means excess, wantonness, the strength that comes from having far more than is needed. Babylon’s hold on the merchants is not that she threatened them. It is that she made them rich.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I heard another voice from heaven saying, "Come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues; for her sins are heaped high as heaven, and God has remembered her iniquities.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I heard another voice from heaven saying, “Come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues.”

The command is quoted from the prophets almost word for word. Jeremiah, of Babylon: Go out of the midst of her, my people! Let every one save his life from the fierce anger of the LORD (Jer. 51:45; cf. 50:8). Isaiah, of the same city: Depart, depart, go out from there; touch no unclean thing (Isa. 52:11). And Paul quoted that line to a church living in a Greek port (2 Cor. 6:17).

Two things need saying about what it does and does not mean, because it has been misused in both directions.

It cannot mean physical withdrawal, and the New Testament settles that. Christians stayed in Rome; Paul greeted a congregation there and told them to pay their taxes. Jesus prayed explicitly not that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one (John 17:15). Paul told the Corinthians that avoiding immoral people altogether would require leaving the world entirely (1 Cor. 5:9–10). Whatever coming out of Babylon is, it is not emigration, and it is not a compound in the hills.

And the verse itself says what it is, twice, in two parallel clauses: lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues. It is non-participation. A Christian lives in the city, works in it, pays for it and prays for it — and does not join in what it does, and does not want what it wants.

Which is far harder than moving house, and far more searching. Nobody has to decide whether to leave a country. Everybody has to decide, repeatedly and in small installments, whether to make the arrangement that everyone makes: the invoice adjusted, the thing not mentioned, the standard that quietly relaxes because it is costing too much. Coming out of Babylon happens on Tuesday afternoons, and nobody photographs it.

And the reason given is the second clause, which is a warning rather than a threat: lest you share in her plagues. Sharing the sins means sharing the judgment. When a system falls, the people who were profiting from it fall with it, and they do not get a separate hearing on the grounds that they were only doing what everyone did.

For her sins are heaped high as heaven, and God has remembered her iniquities.

The image is a tower — sins stacked up until they reach the sky — and it takes the reader straight back to where Babylon began, at a tower whose builders said let us build ourselves a city and a tower with its top in the heavens (Gen. 11:4). She always did want to reach heaven. She has managed it at last, and it is her record that arrived.

And God has remembered, as at 16:19. In Scripture that never means something had slipped his mind. It is the language of a file coming to the top of the pile, and of a God who is about to act on what he has known all along.

verseByVerse.quote: Pay her back as she herself has paid back others, and repay her double for her deeds; mix a double portion for her in the cup she mixed. As she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so give her a like measure of torment and mourning, since in her heart she says, 'I sit as a queen, I am no widow, and mourning I shall never see.' For this reason her plagues will come in a single day, death and mourning and famine, and she will be burned up with fire; for mighty is the Lord God who has judged her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pay her back as she herself has paid back others, and repay her double for her deeds; mix a double portion for her in the cup she mixed.

Two things about that sentence. The addressees are not named — the imperatives are plural and unattributed — and the reader should not assume they are the church, because 17:16 has already said who actually destroys Babylon, and it is the beast and the ten kings. Whoever is being commanded, no Christian in this book ever repays anybody.

And double raises a fair question about justice. If the punishment is twice the crime, is it just? The Hebrew idiom behind it answers that. The word for double (mishneh) is used of a garment folded over so that the two halves match exactly — the second half is not extra, it is the corresponding portion. Isaiah promised Israel a double that plainly meant full compensation rather than excess (Isa. 40:2; 61:7). And the rest of the sentence makes it explicit: mix a double portion for her in the cup she mixed. It is her own cup, her own recipe, folded back on her. Nothing new has been added.

As she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so give her a like measure of torment and mourning, since in her heart she says, ‘I sit as a queen, I am no widow, and mourning I shall never see.’

Here is Babylon in her own words, and the boast is quoted from Isaiah’s taunt against the original city: You said, ‘I shall be mistress for ever’… you who say in your heart, ‘I am, and there is no one besides me; I shall not sit as a widow or know the loss of children’ (Isa. 47:7–8).

Three claims, and each is a denial of something ordinary. I sit as a queen — permanent authority. I am no widow — she will not be left; nothing she depends on can die. Mourning I shall never see — she is exempt from grief.

That is not principally arrogance. It is the settled, unexamined assumption of every prosperous society that has ever existed, and it is why a comfortable church finds this chapter so hard to feel. The claim is not I am better than others; it is this will go on. Anyone who has never seriously reckoned with the possibility that his country, his savings, his health or his arrangements might simply stop has said this sentence in his heart without ever putting it into words.

And Laodicea said the same thing in different vocabulary — I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing (3:17) — which is a warning that the sentence can be said inside a church as easily as inside an empire.

For this reason her plagues will come in a single day, death and mourning and famine, and she will be burned up with fire; for mighty is the Lord God who has judged her.

The three things she said she would never see are the three things that arrive: she will not be a widow, and death comes; she will never see mourning, and mourning comes; she lived in luxury, and famine comes. The judgment is her own boast, itemised and reversed.

In a single day. The chapter will say in a single hour three more times (vv. 10, 17, 19). Something built over centuries goes in an afternoon, which is how these things actually happen — slowly, then all at once.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Three sets of mourners in descending rank, modelled on Ezekiel’s lament over Tyre (Ezek. 26–28). Verses 9–11: the kings weep and wail, stand far off, in fear of her torment, and cry Alas! Alas! You great city… For in a single hour your judgment has come; and the merchants mourn since no one buys their cargo anymore.

Verses 12–13 give the manifest: twenty-eight items in seven groups of four, running downward from precious metals and stones through fabrics, fine furniture, spices, food and livestock — and ending and slaves, that is, human souls. Verse 14 speaks to the city directly: the fruit for which your soul longed has gone from you… never to be found again.

Verses 15–16: the merchants stand far off and describe her as a dressed body — linen, purple, scarlet, gold, jewels, pearls, the wording of 17:4. Verses 17–19: shipmasters, seafaring men and sailors stand far off, throw dust on their heads (cf. Ezek. 27:29–32), and cry What city was like the great city? and in a single hour she has been laid waste.

Verse 20 opens a window in the middle of the funeral: Rejoice over her, O heaven, and you saints and apostles and prophets, for God has given judgment for you against her!
verseByVerse.theology:
“That Is, Human Souls”

John builds twenty-eight items in order to land on the last two words. Slaves is literally bodies, which is how the trade actually spoke; a Roman merchantman’s manifest really would list bodies after livestock. Then John adds four words no manifest ever carried: that is, human souls. It is a correction inserted into somebody else’s paperwork. Perhaps a fifth of the empire was owned, and it is the last thing named before the lament resumes.

The sin named is not wealth. It is an arrangement in which human beings appear on the manifest — where the accounting makes a person a line item, and where the profitability is sufficient reason not to enquire too closely into who is at the far end. Every generation has its version and every generation has found it hard to see while it was running. The question the manifest puts is not whether a reader owns anyone, but whether he knows whose hands made what he is holding, and whether he has ever wanted to.

How Can Heaven Be Told to Rejoice?

The command in v. 20 troubles thoughtful Christians, and four things resolve it without softening the verse. What is celebrated is stated: God has given judgment for you against her — a legal phrase; the joy is over a verdict, not over suffering. Who celebrates is stated: saints and apostles and prophets, and v. 24 says their blood was found in her; nobody who has not been wronged is invited. The alternative is worse than it looks — a universe in which the murder of the innocent is finally shrugged at is not kinder but one in which nothing matters. And the rejoicing follows the judgment and never produces it: no Christian in this book lifts a hand against Babylon.

The Fruit for Which Your Soul Longed

The Greek of v. 14 is the fruit of the desire of your soul — not a word about trade but about appetite. All of it, the silk and the citron wood and the frankincense and the bodies, was built to feed a longing, and the longing was in the soul. That is the diagnosis of what prosperity is usually being asked to do: nobody accumulates in order to have more objects, but because something is hungry and the objects are what is nearest. Augustine said it in a sentence: our hearts are restless until they rest in God. Babylon is that restlessness, organised, with a shipping fleet.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Every item on the manifest is attested in the Roman trade. Silk came overland from China and was worth its weight in gold; Tiberius tried to ban men from wearing it. Citron wood from North Africa made table tops that sold for the price of an estate. Cinnamon and frankincense came up the incense road from Arabia. Rome imported something like a third of a million tons of grain a year because it could not feed itself. The whole world was arranged to supply one city.

Now: One clause governs all three laments and is repeated at vv. 10, 15 and 17: they will stand far off. Nobody goes near. Nobody attempts a rescue. These are her lovers, her business partners and her carriers, and not one of them will cross the road. That is the exact measure of what Babylon’s relationships were worth — and it stands beside the promise made to the poorest church on the road, Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life, said by somebody who did come near.

And read the laments for what is absent from all three. Not one word of repentance. Not one word about the blood of the saints. Not even sympathy for Babylon herself. They weep because they are afraid and because their trade is finished, and v. 11 says so outright: since no one buys their cargo anymore. The most honest sentence in the chapter is in the mouth of the mourners, and they do not seem to notice what they have admitted.

Which puts a plain question to a reader, since Babylon is not only ancient. If the thing you would find hardest to lose were taken away tomorrow, would the grief be for a person or for a market? These men are not condemned for feeling loss. They are shown up by the reason for it.

verseByVerse.quote: And the kings of the earth, who committed sexual immorality and lived in luxury with her, will weep and wail over her when they see the smoke of her burning. They will stand far off, in fear of her torment, and say, "Alas! Alas! You great city, you mighty city, Babylon! For in a single hour your judgment has come." And the merchants of the earth weep and mourn for her, since no one buys their cargo anymore,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the funeral, and it has three sets of mourners in descending order of rank: the kings, the merchants, and the sailors. The whole passage is modelled on Ezekiel’s lament over Tyre, where the same three groups stand off and wail over a burning port (Ezek. 26–28), and John expects the echo to be heard.

And the kings of the earth, who committed sexual immorality and lived in luxury with her, will weep and wail over her when they see the smoke of her burning. They will stand far off, in fear of her torment.

The detail that governs all three laments is in that last clause, and it is repeated at verses 15 and 17: they will stand far off. Nobody goes near. Nobody attempts a rescue. These are her lovers, her business partners and her carriers, and every one of them watches from a safe distance.

That is the exact measure of what Babylon’s relationships were worth. She had the kings of the earth and the merchants of the earth and every shipmaster afloat, and at the end not one of them will cross the road. Set that beside the promise made to the poorest church on the road in chapter 2: Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life — said by somebody who did come near.

And say, “Alas! Alas! You great city, you mighty city, Babylon! For in a single hour your judgment has come.”

The first of the three cries, and each of the three ends the same way — in a single hour. Read the laments carefully and notice what is absent from all three of them. Not one word of repentance. Not one word about the blood of the saints, which verse 24 says was found in her. Not even any sympathy for Babylon herself. They weep because they are afraid, and because their trade is finished.

And the merchants of the earth weep and mourn for her, since no one buys their cargo anymore.

There it is, said outright, and John gives the reason in the same breath as the tears. The merchants are not grieving for a city. They are grieving for a market. The most honest sentence in the chapter is put in the mouth of the mourners, and they do not appear to notice what they have admitted.

And a plain question follows for any reader, since Babylon is not only ancient. If the thing you would find hardest to lose were taken away tomorrow, would the grief be for a person or for a market? The kings and merchants of this chapter are not being condemned for feeling loss. They are being shown up by the reason for it.

verseByVerse.quote: cargo of gold, silver, jewels, pearls, fine linen, purple cloth, silk, scarlet cloth, all kinds of scented wood, all kinds of articles of ivory, all kinds of articles of costly wood, bronze, iron and marble, cinnamon, spice, incense, myrrh, frankincense, wine, oil, fine flour, wheat, cattle and sheep, horses and chariots, and slaves, that is, human souls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the cargo manifest, and it must be read as a list rather than skimmed, because John has arranged it with great care and the last item is the point of the whole chapter.

Cargo of gold, silver, jewels, pearls, fine linen, purple cloth, silk, scarlet cloth, all kinds of scented wood, all kinds of articles of ivory, all kinds of articles of costly wood, bronze, iron and marble, cinnamon, spice, incense, myrrh, frankincense, wine, oil, fine flour, wheat, cattle and sheep, horses and chariots, and slaves, that is, human souls.

Twenty-eight items in seven groups of four — precious metals and stones, fabrics, materials for fine furniture, spices and perfumes, foodstuffs, livestock, and finally people. The order runs downward from the most luxurious to the most basic, which is itself a comment: the list begins with what nobody needs and ends with what everybody does.

The first four items are what the prostitute of chapter 17 was wearing — gold, jewels, pearls, fine linen — and every item on the list is attested in the Roman trade. Silk came overland from China and was worth its weight in gold; Tiberius tried to ban men from wearing it. Citron wood from North Africa made table tops that sold for the price of an estate. Cinnamon and frankincense came up the incense road from Arabia. Rome imported something like a third of a million tons of grain a year from Egypt and Africa because it could not feed itself. The whole world was arranged to supply one city.

And then, at the very end, after the horses and chariots, the last two words of the list: and slaves, that is, human souls.

Stay there, because John has built twenty-eight items in order to land on it. The word translated slaves is literally bodies — which is how the trade actually spoke, and the manifest of a Roman merchantman really would list bodies after livestock. Then John adds four words of his own that no manifest ever carried: that is, human souls.

It is a correction, inserted into somebody else’s paperwork. The market says bodies, in the same column as the cattle, priced by weight and condition. And the apostle stops the list to say what they actually are. Perhaps a fifth of the population of the empire was owned, and it is the last thing named before the lament resumes, and it is the charge that hangs over the entire economy.

Which is why this chapter is not merely about ancient Rome, and why a modern reader should not read it comfortably. The sin named here is not wealth. It is an arrangement in which human beings appear on the manifest — where the accounting is done in a way that makes people into a line item, and where the profitability of the arrangement is sufficient reason not to enquire too closely into who is at the far end of it.

Every generation has its own version, and every generation has found it difficult to see while it was running. The question the manifest puts to a reader is not whether he owns anyone. It is whether he knows whose hands made what he is holding, and whether he has ever wanted to.

verseByVerse.quote: "The fruit for which your soul longed has gone from you, and all your delicacies and your splendors are lost to you, never to be found again!" The merchants of these wares, who gained wealth from her, will stand far off, in fear of her torment, weeping and mourning aloud, "Alas, alas, for the great city that was clothed in fine linen, in purple and scarlet, adorned with gold, with jewels, and with pearls!
verseByVerse.commentary:
“The fruit for which your soul longed has gone from you, and all your delicacies and your splendors are lost to you, never to be found again!”

A single verse spoken directly to the city, breaking into the merchants’ lament — and it contains the most penetrating phrase in the chapter: the fruit for which your soul longed.

The Greek is the fruit of the desire of your soul. It is not a word about trade. It is a word about appetite, and it says that all of this — the silk, the citron wood, the frankincense, the bodies — was never really about commerce at all. It was about wanting. The whole apparatus was built to feed a longing, and the longing was in the soul.

Which is the most useful thing this chapter has to say to a reader in a wealthy society, and it is not an attack on prosperity. It is a diagnosis of what prosperity is usually being asked to do. Nobody accumulates in order to have more objects. People accumulate because something in them is hungry and the objects are what is nearest. Augustine put it in a sentence at the start of his Confessions: our hearts are restless until they rest in God. Babylon is that restlessness, organised, with a shipping fleet.

And the verdict on it is never to be found again. Not merely lost, but unfindable — a phrase that will be repeated over the city three more times before the chapter closes. The fruit her soul longed for did not last, and could not have lasted, and was never going to satisfy the longing even while she had it.

The merchants of these wares, who gained wealth from her, will stand far off, in fear of her torment, weeping and mourning aloud, “Alas, alas, for the great city that was clothed in fine linen, in purple and scarlet, adorned with gold, with jewels, and with pearls!”

The second lament, and it is put in exactly the words used of the woman in 17:4. The merchants describe her as a dressed body: linen, purple, scarlet, gold, jewels, pearls. Six items, and every one of them was for sale in the manifest they have just lost.

So their eulogy for a civilisation is a description of her clothes. They knew her wardrobe and nothing else. There is no mention of anything she did, made, believed or was — and there is nothing else to say, because there was nothing else there.

And once more, the phrase that runs through all three laments: will stand far off. The merchants who gained wealth from her, watching from a distance, mourning aloud, and not moving.

verseByVerse.quote: For in a single hour all this wealth has been laid waste." And all shipmasters and seafaring men, sailors and all whose trade is on the sea, stood far off and cried out as they saw the smoke of her burning, "What city was like the great city?" And they threw dust on their heads as they wept and mourned, crying out, "Alas, alas, for the great city where all who had ships at sea grew rich by her wealth! For in a single hour she has been laid waste.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“For in a single hour all this wealth has been laid waste.” And all shipmasters and seafaring men, sailors and all whose trade is on the sea, stood far off.

The third group, and the humblest: not kings and not merchant princes, but captains, crews and dockworkers — everyone whose living came off the water. Ezekiel’s lament over Tyre has the identical cast standing on the shore, throwing dust on their heads, and crying Who is like Tyre? (Ezek. 27:29–32).

And cried out as they saw the smoke of her burning, “What city was like the great city?”

That question is a parody, and it is the third time this book has used the form. Israel sang at the Red Sea, Who is like you, O LORD, among the gods? (Ex. 15:11). The worshippers of the beast chanted Who is like the beast? (13:4). And here sailors on a beach ask it of a burning city. It is the question of worship, and it keeps being asked of the wrong subject.

And they threw dust on their heads as they wept and mourned, crying out, “Alas, alas, for the great city where all who had ships at sea grew rich by her wealth! For in a single hour she has been laid waste.”

Dust on the head is the ancient sign of grief that has no words left (Josh. 7:6; Job 2:12; Ezek. 27:30). And in a single hour for the third time, from the third group. All three laments say it, which means all three have understood the one thing that actually frightens them: not that Babylon was wicked, but that she was quick.

Consider what that means for anybody whose confidence rests on something built. These are men who have spent their working lives on a trade route, and it took an hour. The chapter is not saying that wealth is evil or that trade is wrong; it is saying that everything in the manifest, and the city that consumed it, and the fleet that carried it, is in the category of things that can end between breakfast and lunch.

And notice that the sailors’ grief is the same as the kings’ and the merchants’, stated in the plainest possible terms: where all who had ships at sea grew rich by her wealth. Three social classes, three laments, and one reason between them. Nobody mourns Babylon. They mourn their share of her.

verseByVerse.quote: Rejoice over her, O heaven, and you saints and apostles and prophets, for God has given judgment for you against her!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rejoice over her, O heaven, and you saints and apostles and prophets, for God has given judgment for you against her!

One verse, and it stands in the middle of the funeral like a window opened in a closed room. Three groups have been weeping; heaven is told to do the opposite.

The command troubles thoughtful Christians, and it should be faced rather than hurried. How can the people of God be told to rejoice over a burning city? Does Scripture not say do not rejoice when your enemy falls (Prov. 24:17), and does God himself not say he has no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezek. 33:11)?

Four things resolve it, and none of them requires softening the verse.

First, look at what they are told to rejoice over. Not suffering, and not destruction as such. The reason is given in the second half of the sentence: for God has given judgment for you against her. The Greek is a legal phrase — he has judged your case. What is being celebrated is a verdict.

Second, consider who is celebrating: saints and apostles and prophets. Chapter 18 ends by saying that in Babylon was found the blood of prophets and of saints. These are the people she killed. Nobody who has not been wronged is invited to this celebration, and there is a great difference between a victim relieved that justice has finally been done and a bystander enjoying somebody’s ruin.

Third, the alternative is worse than it looks. A universe in which the murder of the innocent is finally shrugged at, in which the blood in the foundations of every great city is never mentioned again, is not a kinder universe; it is one in which nothing matters. To be unable to rejoice that wrong has been put right is not compassion. It is a failure to believe that the wrong was real.

Fourth, and this is the safeguard, the rejoicing follows the judgment; it never produces it. No Christian in this book lifts a hand against Babylon. They pray, they endure, they refuse the mark, they die — and God settles the account. The joy of verse 20 is the joy of people who were told to leave it with him and did.

And the verse has a quiet pastoral edge for anyone still carrying something that was never put right — a crime nobody was charged with, a reputation destroyed by somebody who prospered afterwards, a person who died and was never accounted for. This verse says a day is coming when heaven will name your case out loud and tell you to be glad. Not because you were owed revenge, but because you were owed a verdict, and it will be delivered.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–24 — The Millstone and the Sevenfold Silence
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 21: a mighty angel throws a stone like a great millstone into the sea — the act Jeremiah commanded of Seraiah, who tied a stone to the scroll of Babylon’s doom and threw it into the Euphrates saying Thus shall Babylon sink, to rise no more (Jer. 51:59–64). A millstone is the heaviest ordinary object in an ancient town and the last thing in the world that floats.

Verses 22–23 toll the sevenfold silence, six things heard or found no more: the sound of harpists and musicians, flute players and trumpeters; a craftsman of any craft; the sound of the mill; the light of a lamp; and the voice of bridegroom and bride. Jeremiah listed the same three — millstones, lamp, bridegroom and bride — as the sum of what a judged city loses (Jer. 25:10). Two reasons are given: your merchants were the great ones of the earth, and all nations were deceived by your sorcery (pharmakeia, as at 9:21).

Verse 24 gives the indictment: And in her was found the blood of prophets and of saints, and of all who have been slain on earth.
verseByVerse.theology:
What a City Actually Loses

Stand back and see what the sevenfold silence lists. Not palaces, armies, temples or treasuries. Music, craftsmanship, bread, lamplight and weddings. In an ancient town the grinding of the handmills began before dawn and was the ordinary background of being alive — the sound that told you the day had started and there would be bread. The lamp is not a public illumination but the small light in one room where a family sits after dark. And the last is the heaviest: no more weddings means no more future, because nobody is being married, so nobody is being born.

The chapter that spent twelve verses on gold and silk and ivory ends by mourning the mill and the lamp. That is where Babylon’s true wealth was the whole time, and she spent it on cargo.

“All Who Have Been Slain on Earth”

The reach of v. 24 is enormous, and Jesus said something with the same reach over Jerusalem: that on that generation would come all the righteous blood shed on earth, from Abel onward (Matt. 23:35). The logic is not that one city committed every murder. It is that Babylon is the name for the whole arrangement — the human project of building without God, in every century and every place — and every drop of innocent blood was spilled somewhere inside it. The account is presented to the system that produced it.

One Word: “Found”

Babylon did not report it. Somebody looked, and it was there. This is a city that ran the greatest concealment operation in history — brilliant, cultured, generous, beautifully dressed — and at the end the search was conducted anyway and the blood was in the foundations. Nothing was ever really hidden. It was only unlooked-for.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: When a millstone goes into deep water there is one splash and then nothing at all. Jeremiah had a man read the doom of Babylon aloud in Babylon and then sink the scroll in the river, and John’s angel repeats the sign for a second Babylon — thrown down with violence, and will be found no more. The phrase no more or never to be found again falls on this city eight times in eleven verses.

Now: Two diagnoses in v. 23 should be carried out of the chapter. Your merchants were the great ones of the earth is a precise description of what happens when a society decides that money is the only real rank — not that trade is wicked, but that the traders had become the aristocracy. And all nations were deceived by your sorcery uses the word from 9:21: not medicine, but the technique that bends people without their consent. Babylon did not conquer the nations. She persuaded them, and they never noticed being handled.

And the whole chapter puts one question to a reader whose confidence rests on something built. Three social classes, three laments, and every one of them ends in a single hour. These are men who spent their working lives on a trade route, and it took an hour. The chapter does not say wealth is evil or that trade is wrong. It says that everything on the manifest, and the city that consumed it, and the fleet that carried it, is in the category of things that can end between breakfast and lunch — and that the ordinary goods it destroyed, the bread and the lamp and the wedding, were worth more than the cargo all along.

verseByVerse.quote: Then a mighty angel took up a stone like a great millstone and threw it into the sea, saying, "So will Babylon the great city be thrown down with violence, and will be found no more; and the sound of harpists and musicians, of flute players and trumpeters, will be heard in you no more, and a craftsman of any craft will be found in you no more, and the sound of the mill will be heard in you no more, and the light of a lamp will shine in you no more, and the voice of bridegroom and bride will be heard in you no more, for your merchants were the great ones of the earth, and all nations were deceived by your sorcery. And in her was found the blood of prophets and of saints, and of all who have been slain on earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then a mighty angel took up a stone like a great millstone and threw it into the sea, saying, “So will Babylon the great city be thrown down with violence, and will be found no more.”

The act is borrowed from Jeremiah, and John expects it to be known. Jeremiah wrote all the disaster coming on Babylon in a book, gave it to a man named Seraiah, and told him that when he had finished reading it aloud in Babylon he should tie a stone to it and throw it into the Euphrates and say Thus shall Babylon sink, to rise no more (Jer. 51:59–64).

A millstone is the right object for it. It is the heaviest ordinary thing in an ancient town, the stone an animal turned all day to grind the community’s grain, and it is the last thing in the world that floats. When it goes into deep water there is one splash and then nothing at all.

Then the sevenfold silence, and it is the most beautiful and most desolating passage in the chapter. Six things will be heard or found no more, and the phrase itself tolls six times.

The sound of harpists and musicians, of flute players and trumpeters, will be heard in you no more. Music goes first. No concerts, no weddings, no processions, nobody practising badly through an open window.

And a craftsman of any craft will be found in you no more. No workshops. Nobody making anything. The particular satisfaction of skilled hands producing something that did not exist before is gone from the whole city.

And the sound of the mill will be heard in you no more. The stone that was just thrown into the sea. In an ancient town the grinding of the handmills began before dawn and was the ordinary background of being alive — the sound that told you the day had started and there would be bread. Jeremiah listed its ending among the worst things God would do (Jer. 25:10).

And the light of a lamp will shine in you no more. Not a public illumination — a lamp, the small light in one room where a family sits after dark. Every window in the city, black.

And the voice of bridegroom and bride will be heard in you no more. This is the last and the heaviest. No more weddings, which means no more future: nobody is being married, so nobody is being born, so there will be no next generation. Jeremiah used exactly this pair of images together — the voice of the bridegroom and the bride, and the sound of the millstones, and the light of the lamp — as the sum of everything a judged city loses (Jer. 25:10).

Stand back and see what has been listed. Not palaces, armies, temples or treasuries. Music, craftsmanship, bread, lamplight and weddings. The things named are the ordinary goods of human life, and the chapter that has spent twelve verses on gold and silk and ivory ends by mourning the loss of the mill and the lamp. That is where Babylon’s true wealth was the whole time, and she spent it on cargo.

Two reasons are given. For your merchants were the great ones of the earth — the traders had become the aristocracy, which is a precise description of what happens when a society decides that money is the only real rank. And all nations were deceived by your sorcery — pharmakeia again, the word used at 9:21: manipulation, the technique that bends people without their consent.

And in her was found the blood of prophets and of saints, and of all who have been slain on earth.

The last verse is the indictment, and it is enormous. Not merely the blood of the martyrs she killed herself — all who have been slain on earth. Jesus said something with the same reach over Jerusalem: that on that generation would come all the righteous blood shed on earth, from Abel onward (Matt. 23:35).

The logic is not that one city committed every murder. It is that Babylon is the name for the whole arrangement — the human project of building without God, in every century and every place — and every drop of innocent blood ever spilled was spilled somewhere inside it. The account is presented to the system that produced it.

And a single word in that verse should not be passed over. Found. Babylon did not report it. Somebody looked, and it was there. This is a city that ran the greatest concealment operation in history — brilliant, cultured, generous, beautifully dressed — and at the end the search was conducted anyway and the blood was in the foundations. Nothing was ever really hidden. It was only unlooked-for.

She has become a dwelling place for demons, a haunt for every unclean spirit, a haunt for every unclean bird, a haunt for every unclean and detestable beast.<sup>3</sup>For all nations have drunk the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality, and the kings of the earth have committed immorality with her, and the merchants of the earth have grown rich from the power of her luxurious living.”<sup>4</sup>Then I heard another voice from heaven saying, “Come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues;<sup>5</sup>for her sins are heaped high as heaven, and God has remembered her iniquities.<sup>6</sup>Pay her back as she herself has paid back others, and repay her double for her deeds; mix a double portion for her in the cup she mixed.<sup>7</sup>As she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so give her a like measure of torment and mourning, since in her heart she says, ‘I sit as a queen, I am no widow, and mourning I shall never see.’<sup>8</sup>For this reason her plagues will come in a single day, death and mourning and famine, and she will be burned up with fire; for mighty is the Lord God who has judged her.”<sup>9</sup>And the kings of the earth, who committed sexual immorality and lived in luxury with her, will weep and wail over her when they see the smoke of her burning.<sup>10</sup>They will stand far off, in fear of her torment, and say, “Alas!
